Doublets stores the links themselves.\n  The operations are create, read all, read by id, search by `(from, to)`,\n  read by `from`, read by `to`, update (swap `from` and `to`) and delete.\n- **Objects**: blog posts with a title, content and publication date. SQLite\n  stores the table `blog_posts(id, title, content, publication_date)`;\n  Doublets stores every post as links, with strings as sequences of Unicode\n  symbols, like\n  [Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences](https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets.Sequences)\n  does. The operations are create, read all, read by id and delete. Every\n  Doublets store runs with and without a cache of the string sequences\n  (`Cached`/`Uncached`).\n\nStorages: SQLite in memory and in a file; Doublets united (one array of links\nwith index trees) and split (separate data and index arrays), each volatile\n(in memory) and non-volatile (in memory-mapped files). Doublets are compared\nwith SQLite of the same durability: volatile with `SQLite Memory`,\nnon-volatile with `SQLite File`.\n\nC# also runs `SystemDataSQLite_Memory` and `SystemDataSQLite_File` with\nSystem.Data.SQLite 2.0.4. `SQLite_Memory` and `SQLite_File` use\nMicrosoft.Data.Sqlite. Both providers use the same schemas, parameterized\ncommands, immediate transactions and native `e_sqlite3` library supplied by\nMicrosoft.Data.Sqlite, on Linux, macOS and Windows. The JSON reports record\neach provider and engine version in `sqlite_providers`. The System.Data.SQLite\nrows compare with Microsoft.Data.Sqlite of the same durability. Published\ntables from older runs include only the providers measured in those runs;\nthe next Benchmarks run adds the new rows.\n\nC# object benchmarks also support `PostgreSQL_EFCore` using\n[Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL](https://www.npgsql.org/efcore/).\nSet `POSTGRESQL_CONNECTION_STRING` to include it in the default object comparison;\nembedded benchmarks work without a PostgreSQL server. Explicitly selecting it\nwithout configuration fails with a setup message. Both id widths use the same\ndeterministic posts, scattered point reads, validated operations, warm-ups and\ntransaction boundaries as the other object stores. EF saves one post at a time,\nclears tracking after each save, reads without tracking and deletes by id.\nEach warm-up and repetition creates and drops its own generated schema; the\ndatabase and other schemas remain intact. The configured user needs permission\nto connect and create schemas in a benchmark database.\n\nPostgreSQL is a server database and EF Core adds ORM and network costs. Its row\nshows absolute timings without an embedded-storage speed ratio. `server_bytes`\nmeasures the benchmark table, indexes and TOAST storage after creation, shown in\na separate server-relations column; it excludes shared WAL, server memory and\nlocal client files. JSON and generated tables record PostgreSQL, Npgsql EF Core\nand EF Core versions. Existing published measurements stay intact. CI adds a\npinned PostgreSQL service to each C# object benchmark job so all compared\nvariants still run on the same machine. Set `POSTGRESQL_VERBOSE=1` to log EF\ndiagnostics to stderr; logging is off by default and sensitive values are disabled.\n\nEvery repetition runs on a fresh store in an empty directory, after discarded\nwarm-up repetitions on up to 10,000 records that run for at least a second, so\nthe .NET JIT has already optimized the code. Each operation is one\ntimed transaction over all records, point operations visit the records in a\nscattered order, and each result is checked against the expected count and\norder-sensitive checksum, so a storage that loses, duplicates or mixes up\nrecords fails the run instead of being reported as fast. Repetitions are\n`3,000,000 / size` for links and `500,000 / size` for objects, clamped to\n`1..=10`. The tables show the median time per operation; a difference is\nreported only if the interquartile ranges (the middle half) of the\nrepetitions do not overlap and the medians differ by more than 5%, otherwise\nit is `≈ same`. The file size is measured after creation; Doublets files are\npreallocated memory-mapped files, so small stores show the preallocation size.\n\nEach results group includes linear and logarithmic charts. Linear charts raise\nbars below 0.5% of the panel maximum for visibility; the tables retain exact\ntimes. Provenance records the Doublets library and Rust compiler or .NET SDK\nversions used for that run. Older reports without this metadata identify it\nas missing rather than attributing current toolchains to past measurements.\n\nEvery table is measured by its own GitHub Actions job, with all variants on\nthe same runner, so that a difference is never a difference between machines,\nby the [Benchmarks workflow](.github/workflows/benchmarks.yml): links with\n100,000, 1,000,000 and 10,000,000 records and objects with 100,000 and\n1,000,000 records. These are the largest sizes that fit into the 6 hour limit\nof a job: one SQLite File repetition on 100,000,000 links did not finish in\n4.5 hours\n([run 37228604862](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/37228604862)),\nand 1,000,000 blog posts already take an hour in C#. Pull requests check the\nwhole pipeline on 1,000 records, and pushes to `main` update the results below.\nThe workflow can also be started manually with other sizes.\n\nRun locally:\n\n```bash\nmkdir -p results\ncargo run --release --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -- \\\n  links 64 100000 --output results/links-rust-64-100000.json\ndotnet run -c Release --project csharp/SQLiteVSDoublets -- \\\n  objects 32 1000 --variants SQLite_File,Doublets_Split_NonVolatile_Cached\ndotnet run -c Release --project csharp/SQLiteVSDoublets -- \\\n  links 64 1000 --repetitions 3 \\\n  --variants SQLite_Memory,SystemDataSQLite_Memory \\\n  --output results/links-csharp-64-1000.json\npython3 scripts/benchmark_provenance.py results/links-rust-64-100000.json \\\n  --toolchain \"$(rustc --version)\"\npython3 scripts/benchmark_provenance.py results/links-csharp-64-1000.json \\\n  --toolchain \".NET SDK $(dotnet --version)\"\n# print the tables, add --readme README.md --charts docs/benchmarks to update\npython3 scripts/benchmark_report.py results\n```\n\nRun a bounded PostgreSQL comparison:\n\n```bash\ndocker run -d --name benchmark-postgres -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 \\\n  -e POSTGRES_USER=benchmark -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=[REDACTED] \\\n  -e POSTGRES_DB=benchmark postgres:18.3\nexport POSTGRESQL_CONNECTION_STRING='Host=127.0.0.1;Database=benchmark;Username=benchmark;Password=[REDACTED]'\ndotnet run -c Release --project csharp/SQLiteVSDoublets -- \\\n  objects 64 1000 --repetitions 3 \\\n  --variants SQLite_Memory,SQLite_File,PostgreSQL_EFCore \\\n  --output results/objects-csharp-64-1000.json\npython3 scripts/benchmark_report.py results\npython3 experiments/postgresql/check_reports.py\ndocker stop benchmark-postgres\ndocker rm benchmark-postgres\n```\n\nNotes:\n\n- The split stores of doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) lose a link that is updated to\n  reference itself, so the benchmark updates a link to `(0, 0)` first, which\n  is the state links are created in\n  ([experiments/split_store_delete](experiments/split_store_delete)).\n- The stores of doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) take the part of the memory that\n  `platform-mem` 0.3.0 returns after growing it for the whole memory, so a\n  store fails after 1,040,384 links; the benchmarks wrap the memory in\n  [`memory::Whole`](rust/src/memory.rs), which returns the whole memory\n  ([experiments/unit_store_growth](experiments/unit_store_growth)).\n- In C#, links are deleted with `Delete(id, handler: null)`, which resets the\n  link before deleting it; the bare `Delete(id)` leaves the link in the index\n  trees, and later searches fail\n  ([experiments/csharp_tree_delete](experiments/csharp_tree_delete)).\n- The C# united stores use AVL index trees: the default size balanced trees\n  degenerate when many links share a source or a target, which makes each\n  blog post creation linear in the number of posts\n  ([experiments/csharp_objects_profile](experiments/csharp_objects_profile)).\n- The C# split stores keep the default linked list of the internal sources,\n  which doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) does not have; it makes the C# updates faster\n  and the other operations take about the same time\n  ([experiments/csharp_split_linked_list](experiments/csharp_split_linked_list)).\n- Objects stores use external references for numbers and Unicode symbols, so\n  raw values never collide with link ids.\n- Reading a string without the cache walks its sequence link by link; in C#\n  each `GetSource`/`GetTarget` call of `Platform.Data` allocates a handler and\n  a list, which makes the uncached C# reads much slower than the Rust ones.\n\n<!--BENCHMARK_RESULTS_START-->\n<!-- markdownlint-disable MD013 MD024 -->\n## Doublets vs SQLite as storage for links\n\n### Rust doublets vs SQLite\n\n#### 32 [2026-11-25T10:28:39.545Z] [INFO]         "content": "# Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets ([русская версия](README.ru.md))\n\n[![Rust](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/workflows/rust.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/workflows/rust.yml)\n[![C#](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/workflows/csharp.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/workflows/csharp.yml)\n[![Benchmarks](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/workflows/benchmarks.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/workflows/benchmarks.yml)\n\n![Comparison of models](https://github.com/LinksPlatform/Documentation/raw/master/doc/ModelsComparison/relational_model_vs_associative_model_vs_links.png)\n\nComparison of SQLite and LinksPlatform's Doublets (links) on basic embedded\ndatabase operations with links and object-like structures.\n\nBased on examples from <https://github.com/FahaoTang/dotnetcore-examples> and\n<https://github.com/Konard/LinksPlatform>\n\n## Benchmarks\n\nRust ([doublets](https://crates.io/crates/doublets) and\n[rusqlite](https://crates.io/crates/rusqlite) with bundled SQLite) and C#\n([Platform.Data.Doublets](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Platform.Data.Doublets),\n[Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences)\nand the providers [Microsoft.Data.Sqlite](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.Data.Sqlite)\nand [System.Data.SQLite](https://www.nuget.org/packages/System.Data.SQLite))\nrun the same workloads on the same deterministic data, with 32 bit\n(`u32`/`uint`) and 64 bit (`u64`/`ulong`) ids:\n\n- **Links**: SQLite stores the table\n  `links(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, \"from\", \"to\")` with the indices\n  `(\"from\", \"to\")` and `(\"to\", \"from\")`; Doublets stores the links themselves.\n  The operations are create, read all, read by id, search by `(from, to)`,\n  read by `from`, read by `to`, update (swap `from` and `to`) and delete.\n- **Objects**: blog posts with a title, content and publication date. SQLite\n  stores the table `blog_posts(id, title, content, publication_date)`;\n  Doublets stores every post as links, with strings as sequences of Unicode\n  symbols, like\n  [Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences](https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets.Sequences)\n  does. The operations are create, read all, read by id and delete. Every\n  Doublets store runs with and without a cache of the string sequences\n  (`Cached`/`Uncached`).\n\nStorages: SQLite in memory and in a file; Doublets united (one array of links\nwith index trees) and split (separate data and index arrays), each volatile\n(in memory) and non-volatile (in memory-mapped files). Doublets are compared\nwith SQLite of the same durability: volatile with `SQLite Memory`,\nnon-volatile with `SQLite File`.\n\nC# also runs `SystemDataSQLite_Memory` and `SystemDataSQLite_File` with\nSystem.Data.SQLite 2.0.4. `SQLite_Memory` and `SQLite_File` use\nMicrosoft.Data.Sqlite. Both providers use the same schemas, parameterized\ncommands, immediate transactions and native `e_sqlite3` library supplied by\nMicrosoft.Data.Sqlite, on Linux, macOS and Windows. The JSON reports record\neach provider and engine version in `sqlite_providers`. The System.Data.SQLite\nrows compare with Microsoft.Data.Sqlite of the same durability. Published\ntables from older runs include only the providers measured in those runs;\nthe next Benchmarks run adds the new rows.\n\nC# object benchmarks also support `PostgreSQL_EFCore` using\n[Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL](https://www.npgsql.org/efcore/).\nSet `POSTGRESQL_CONNECTION_STRING` to include it in the default object comparison;\nembedded benchmarks work without a PostgreSQL server. Explicitly selecting it\nwithout configuration fails with a setup message. Both id widths use the same\ndeterministic posts, scattered point reads, validated operations, warm-ups and\ntransaction boundaries as the other object stores. EF saves one post at a time,\nclears tracking after each save, reads without tracking and deletes by id.\nEach warm-up and repetition creates and drops its own generated schema; the\ndatabase and other schemas remain intact. The configured user needs permission\nto connect and create schemas in a benchmark database.\n\nPostgreSQL is a server database and EF Core adds ORM and network costs. Its row\nshows absolute timings without an embedded-storage speed ratio. `server_bytes`\nmeasures the benchmark table, indexes and TOAST storage after creation, shown in\na separate server-relations column; it excludes shared WAL, server memory and\nlocal client files. JSON and generated tables record PostgreSQL, Npgsql EF Core\nand EF Core versions. Existing published measurements stay intact. CI adds a\npinned PostgreSQL service to each C# object benchmark job so all compared\nvariants still run on the same machine. Set `POSTGRESQL_VERBOSE=1` to log EF\ndiagnostics to stderr; logging is off by default and sensitive values are disabled.\n\nEvery repetition runs on a fresh store in an empty directory, after discarded\nwarm-up repetitions on up to 10,000 records that run for at least a second, so\nthe .NET JIT has already optimized the code. Each operation is one\ntimed transaction over all records, point operations visit the records in a\nscattered order, and each result is checked against the expected count and\norder-sensitive checksum, so a storage that loses, duplicates or mixes up\nrecords fails the run instead of being reported as fast. Repetitions are\n`3,000,000 / size` for links and `500,000 / size` for objects, clamped to\n`1..=10`. The tables show the median time per operation; a difference is\nreported only if the interquartile ranges (the middle half) of the\nrepetitions do not overlap and the medians differ by more than 5%, otherwise\nit is `≈ same`. The file size is measured after creation; Doublets files are\npreallocated memory-mapped files, so small stores show the preallocation size.\n\nEach results group includes linear and logarithmic charts. Linear charts raise\nbars below 0.5% of the panel maximum for visibility; the tables retain exact\ntimes. Provenance records the Doublets library and Rust compiler or .NET SDK\nversions used for that run. Older reports without this metadata identify it\nas missing rather than attributing current toolchains to past measurements.\n\nEvery table is measured by its own GitHub Actions job, with all variants on\nthe same runner, so that a difference is never a difference between machines,\nby the [Benchmarks workflow](.github/workflows/benchmarks.yml): links with\n100,000, 1,000,000 and 10,000,000 records and objects with 100,000 and\n1,000,000 records. These are the largest sizes that fit into the 6 hour limit\nof a job: one SQLite File repetition on 100,000,000 links did not finish in\n4.5 hours\n([run 37228604862](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/37228604862)),\nand 1,000,000 blog posts already take an hour in C#. Pull requests check the\nwhole pipeline on 1,000 records, and pushes to `main` update the results below.\nThe workflow can also be started manually with other sizes.\n\nRun locally:\n\n```bash\nmkdir -p results\ncargo run --release --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -- \\\n  links 64 100000 --output results/links-rust-64-100000.json\ndotnet run -c Release --project csharp/SQLiteVSDoublets -- \\\n  objects 32 1000 --variants SQLite_File,Doublets_Split_NonVolatile_Cached\ndotnet run -c Release --project csharp/SQLiteVSDoublets -- \\\n  links 64 1000 --repetitions 3 \\\n  --variants SQLite_Memory,SystemDataSQLite_Memory \\\n  --output results/links-csharp-64-1000.json\npython3 scripts/benchmark_provenance.py results/links-rust-64-100000.json \\\n  --toolchain \"$(rustc --version)\"\npython3 scripts/benchmark_provenance.py results/links-csharp-64-1000.json \\\n  --toolchain \".NET SDK $(dotnet --version)\"\n# print the tables, add --readme README.md --charts docs/benchmarks to update\npython3 scripts/benchmark_report.py results\n```\n\nRun a bounded PostgreSQL comparison:\n\n```bash\ndocker run -d --name benchmark-postgres -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 \\\n  -e POSTGRES_USER=benchmark -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=[REDACTED] \\\n  -e POSTGRES_DB=benchmark postgres:18.3\nexport POSTGRESQL_CONNECTION_STRING='Host=127.0.0.1;Database=benchmark;Username=benchmark;Password=[REDACTED]'\ndotnet run -c Release --project csharp/SQLiteVSDoublets -- \\\n  objects 64 1000 --repetitions 3 \\\n  --variants SQLite_Memory,SQLite_File,PostgreSQL_EFCore \\\n  --output results/objects-csharp-64-1000.json\npython3 scripts/benchmark_report.py results\npython3 experiments/postgresql/check_reports.py\ndocker stop benchmark-postgres\ndocker rm benchmark-postgres\n```\n\nNotes:\n\n- The split stores of doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) lose a link that is updated to\n  reference itself, so the benchmark updates a link to `(0, 0)` first, which\n  is the state links are created in\n  ([experiments/split_store_delete](experiments/split_store_delete)).\n- The stores of doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) take the part of the memory that\n  `platform-mem` 0.3.0 returns after growing it for the whole memory, so a\n  store fails after 1,040,384 links; the benchmarks wrap the memory in\n  [`memory::Whole`](rust/src/memory.rs), which returns the whole memory\n  ([experiments/unit_store_growth](experiments/unit_store_growth)).\n- In C#, links are deleted with `Delete(id, handler: null)`, which resets the\n  link before deleting it; the bare `Delete(id)` leaves the link in the index\n  trees, and later searches fail\n  ([experiments/csharp_tree_delete](experiments/csharp_tree_delete)).\n- The C# united stores use AVL index trees: the default size balanced trees\n  degenerate when many links share a source or a target, which makes each\n  blog post creation linear in the number of posts\n  ([experiments/csharp_objects_profile](experiments/csharp_objects_profile)).\n- The C# split stores keep the default linked list of the internal sources,\n  which doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) does not have; it makes the C# updates faster\n  and the other operations take about the same time\n  ([experiments/csharp_split_linked_list](experiments/csharp_split_linked_list)).\n- Objects stores use external references for numbers and Unicode symbols, so\n  raw values never collide with link ids.\n- Reading a string without the cache walks its sequence link by link; in C#\n  each `GetSource`/`GetTarget` call of `Platform.Data` allocates a handler and\n  a list, which makes the uncached C# reads much slower than the Rust ones.\n\n<!--BENCHMARK_RESULTS_START-->\n<!-- markdownlint-disable MD013 MD024 -->\n## Doublets vs SQLite as storage for links\n\n### Rust doublets vs SQLite\n\n#### 32 Doublets are compared\nwith SQLite of the same durability: volatile with `SQLite Memory`,\nnon-volatile with `SQLite File`.\n\nC# also runs `SystemDataSQLite_Memory` and `SystemDataSQLite_File` with\nSystem.Data.SQLite 2.0.4. `SQLite_Memory` and `SQLite_File` use\nMicrosoft.Data.Sqlite. Both providers use the same schemas, parameterized\ncommands, immediate transactions and native `e_sqlite3` library supplied by\nMicrosoft.Data.Sqlite, on Linux, macOS and Windows. The JSON reports record\neach provider and engine version in `sqlite_providers`. The System.Data.SQLite\nrows compare with Microsoft.Data.Sqlite of the same durability. Published\ntables from older runs include only the providers measured in those runs;\nthe next Benchmarks run adds the new rows.\n\nC# object benchmarks also support `PostgreSQL_EFCore` using\n[Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL](https://www.npgsql.org/efcore/).\nSet `POSTGRESQL_CONNECTION_STRING` to include it in the default object comparison;\nembedded benchmarks work without a PostgreSQL server. Explicitly selecting it\nwithout configuration fails with a setup message. Both id widths use the same\ndeterministic posts, scattered point reads, validated operations, warm-ups and\ntransaction boundaries as the other object stores. EF saves one post at a time,\nclears tracking after each save, reads without tracking and deletes by id.\nEach warm-up and repetition creates and drops its own generated schema; the\ndatabase and other schemas remain intact. The configured user needs permission\nto connect and create schemas in a benchmark database.\n\nPostgreSQL is a server database and EF Core adds ORM and network costs. Its row\nshows absolute timings without an embedded-storage speed ratio. `server_bytes`\nmeasures the benchmark table, indexes and TOAST storage after creation, shown in\na separate server-relations column; it excludes shared WAL, server memory and\nlocal client files. JSON and generated tables record PostgreSQL, Npgsql EF Core\nand EF Core versions. Existing published measurements stay intact. CI adds a\npinned PostgreSQL service to each C# object benchmark job so all compared\nvariants still run on the same machine. Set `POSTGRESQL_VERBOSE=1` to log EF\ndiagnostics to stderr; logging is off by default and sensitive values are disabled.\n\nEvery repetition runs on a fresh store in an empty directory, after discarded\nwarm-up repetitions on up to 10,000 records that run for at least a second, so\nthe .NET JIT has already optimized the code. Each operation is one\ntimed transaction over all records, point operations visit the records in a\nscattered order, and each result is checked against the expected count and\norder-sensitive checksum, so a storage that loses, duplicates or mixes up\nrecords fails the run instead of being reported as fast. Repetitions are\n`3,000,000 / size` for links and `500,000 / size` for objects, clamped to\n`1..=10`. The tables show the median time per operation; a difference is\nreported only if the interquartile ranges (the middle half) of the\nrepetitions do not overlap and the medians differ by more than 5%, otherwise\nit is `≈ same`. The file size is measured after creation; Doublets files are\npreallocated memory-mapped files, so small stores show the preallocation size.\n\nEach results group includes linear and logarithmic charts. Linear charts raise\nbars below 0.5% of the panel maximum for visibility; the tables retain exact\ntimes. Provenance records the Doublets library and Rust compiler or .NET SDK\nversions used for that run. Older reports without this metadata identify it\nas missing rather than attributing current toolchains to past measurements.\n\nEvery table is measured by its own GitHub Actions job, with all variants on\nthe same runner, so that a difference is never a difference between machines,\nby the [Benchmarks workflow](.github/workflows/benchmarks.yml): links with\n100,000, 1,000,000 and 10,000,000 records and objects with 100,000 and\n1,000,000 records. These are the largest sizes that fit into the 6 hour limit\nof a job: one SQLite File repetition on 100,000,000 links did not finish in\n4.5 hours\n([run 37228604862](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/37228604862)),\nand 1,000,000 blog posts already take an hour in C#. Pull requests check the\nwhole pipeline on 1,000 records, and pushes to `main` update the results below.\nThe workflow can also be started manually with other sizes.\n\nRun locally:\n\n```bash\nmkdir -p results\ncargo run --release --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -- \\\n  links 64 100000 --output results/links-rust-64-100000.json\ndotnet run -c Release --project csharp/SQLiteVSDoublets -- \\\n  objects 32 1000 --variants SQLite_File,Doublets_Split_NonVolatile_Cached\ndotnet run -c Release --project csharp/SQLiteVSDoublets -- \\\n  links 64 1000 --repetitions 3 \\\n  --variants SQLite_Memory,SystemDataSQLite_Memory \\\n  --output results/links-csharp-64-1000.json\npython3 scripts/benchmark_provenance.py results/links-rust-64-100000.json \\\n  --toolchain \"$(rustc --version)\"\npython3 scripts/benchmark_provenance.py results/links-csharp-64-1000.json \\\n  --toolchain \".NET SDK $(dotnet --version)\"\n# print the tables, add --readme README.md --charts docs/benchmarks to update\npython3 scripts/benchmark_report.py results\n```\n\nRun a bounded PostgreSQL comparison:\n\n```bash\ndocker run -d --name benchmark-postgres -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 \\\n  -e POSTGRES_USER=benchmark -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=[REDACTED] \\\n  -e POSTGRES_DB=benchmark postgres:18.3\nexport POSTGRESQL_CONNECTION_STRING='Host=127.0.0.1;Database=benchmark;Username=benchmark;Password=[REDACTED]'\ndotnet run -c Release --project csharp/SQLiteVSDoublets -- \\\n  objects 64 1000 --repetitions 3 \\\n  --variants SQLite_Memory,SQLite_File,PostgreSQL_EFCore \\\n  --output results/objects-csharp-64-1000.json\npython3 scripts/benchmark_report.py results\npython3 experiments/postgresql/check_reports.py\ndocker stop benchmark-postgres\ndocker rm benchmark-postgres\n```\n\nNotes:\n\n- The split stores of doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) lose a link that is updated to\n  reference itself, so the benchmark updates a link to `(0, 0)` first, which\n  is the state links are created in\n  ([experiments/split_store_delete](experiments/split_store_delete)).\n- The stores of doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) take the part of the memory that\n  `platform-mem` 0.3.0 returns after growing it for the whole memory, so a\n  store fails after 1,040,384 links; the benchmarks wrap the memory in\n  [`memory::Whole`](rust/src/memory.rs), which returns the whole memory\n  ([experiments/unit_store_growth](experiments/unit_store_growth)).\n- In C#, links are deleted with `Delete(id, handler: null)`, which resets the\n  link before deleting it; the bare `Delete(id)` leaves the link in the index\n  trees, and later searches fail\n  ([experiments/csharp_tree_delete](experiments/csharp_tree_delete)).\n- The C# united stores use AVL index trees: the default size balanced trees\n  degenerate when many links share a source or a target, which makes each\n  blog post creation linear in the number of posts\n  ([experiments/csharp_objects_profile](experiments/csharp_objects_profile)).\n- The C# split stores keep the default linked list of the internal sources,\n  which doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) does not have; it makes the C# updates faster\n  and the other operations take about the same time\n  ([experiments/csharp_split_linked_list](experiments/csharp_split_linked_list)).\n- Objects stores use external references for numbers and Unicode symbols, so\n  raw values never collide with link ids.\n- Reading a string without the cache walks its sequence link by link; in C#\n  each `GetSource`/`GetTarget` call of `Platform.Data` allocates a handler and\n  a list, which makes the uncached C# reads much slower than the Rust ones.\n\n<!--BENCHMARK_RESULTS_START-->\n<!-- markdownlint-disable MD013 MD024 -->\n## Doublets vs SQLite as storage for links\n\n### Rust doublets vs SQLite\n\n#### 32 Rust implementation of Doublets (associative storage links).\n\nRust port of [Data.Doublets](https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets) library.\n\n## Overview\n\nDoublets is an associative data structure that represents a link store where each link consists of:\n- **Index** - unique identifier of the link\n- **Source** - the link's source (can reference itself or another link)\n- **Target** - the link's target (can reference itself or another link)\n\nThis simple yet powerful structure can represent any data model, from traditional key-value pairs to complex graph structures. Doublets provide a unified approach to data storage with constant-time lookup operations using size-balanced trees.\n\n### Key Features\n\n- **File-mapped storage** - data persists directly to disk using memory-mapped files\n- **Generic link types** - supports any unsigned integer type (`u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `usize`)\n- **Two storage modes**:\n  - `unit::Store` - combined data and index storage in a single memory region\n  - `split::Store` - separated data and index storage for optimized memory layouts\n- **Thread-safe** - `Send` and `Sync` implementations for concurrent access\n- **Query system** - flexible pattern matching using `any` constants\n- **FFI bindings** - C-compatible foreign function interface for cross-language integration\n\n## Deletion and release\n\n`delete*` methods retain automatic endpoint reset as a checked convenience.\nFor an already reset live link, `doublets::mem::Release::release` releases its\nslot without another update. `CheckedRelease` offers the same release-only\nbehavior in decorator stacks; adding `NonNullContentsLinkDeletionResolver`\nexplicitly enables resetting. An unsafe primitive is available to callers that\ncan guarantee the release contract. Incoming references remain valid in both\nlayouts, including after address reuse. See [deletion and release](docs/deletion.md)\nfor contracts, examples, callbacks and usage policies.\n\n## Checked and unchecked mutation\n\nThe safe `update*` and `delete*` methods of both stores reject a missing address\nwith `Error::NotExists`. They leave the store unchanged and make no callback.\nThat check is the explicit `decorators::CheckedMutation` adapter. A caller that\nalready guarantees a live address can omit it by calling\n`unsafe doublets::mem::UncheckedMutation::update_unchecked` and\n`Release::release_unchecked`. To ignore a missing deletion instead of returning\nan error, add `NonExistentDeletionResolver`; it never swallows unrelated errors.\nSee [checked and unchecked mutation](docs/mutation.md) for the preconditions and\nthe routes.\n\n## Installation\n\nAdd to your `Cargo.toml`:\n\n```toml\n[dependencies]\ndoublets = \"0.21.0\"\n```\n\nUse stable Rust 1.85 or newer. The repository's `rust-toolchain.toml` selects the\nstable channel, and the crate declares `rust-version = \"1.85\"` in\n`doublets/Cargo.toml`.\n\n```bash\nrustup toolchain install stable\ncargo +stable build\n```\n\nFor source checkouts, standalone FFI builds, and troubleshooting older nightly\ndependency errors, see [Stable Rust Support](STABLE_RUST.md).\n\nTo depend on the current Git source instead of a crates.io release:\n\n```toml\n[dependencies]\ndoublets = { git = \"https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs\", branch = \"main\" }\n```\n\nBoth sources build on stable Rust. If a Git dependency still reports the old\n`impl Trait` or unknown-feature errors from\n[issue 19](https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/issues/19), follow the\n[Git dependency troubleshooting steps](STABLE_RUST.md#git-dependencies-and-issue-19).\n\n## Example\n\nBasic CRUD operations with doublets:\n\n```rust\nuse doublets::{mem, unit, Doublets, DoubletsExt, Link, Links};\nuse data::Flow;\n\nfn main() -> Result<(), doublets::Error<usize>> {\n    // Use file as persistent storage for doublets\n    let mem = mem::FileMapped::from_path(\"db.links\")?;\n    let mut store = unit::Store::<usize, _>::new(mem)?;\n\n    // Create a point link (a link that references itself as both source and target)\n    // Point: 1 -> (1, 1)\n    let point = store.create_point()?;\n    println!(\"Created point: {}\", point);\n\n    // Create a regular link with explicit source and target\n    // Link: 2 -> (1, 1)\n    let link = store.create_link(point, point)?;\n    println!(\"Created link: {}\", link);\n\n    // The `any` constant matches any link in queries\n    let any = store.constants().any;\n\n    // Count all links in the store\n    println!(\"Total links: {}\", store.count());\n\n    // Iterate over all links using pattern [any, any, any]\n    println!(\"All links:\");\n    store.each_iter([any, any, any]).for_each(|link| {\n        println!(\"  {}: {} -> {}\", link.index, link.source, link.target);\n    });\nShell cwd was reset to /tmp/gh-issue-solver-1795602421354",

Rust implementation of Doublets (associative storage links).\n\nRust port of [Data.Doublets](https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets) library.\n\n## Overview\n\nDoublets is an associative data structure that represents a link store where each link consists of:\n- **Index** - unique identifier of the link\n- **Source** - the link's source (can reference itself or another link)\n- **Target** - the link's target (can reference itself or another link)\n\nThis simple yet powerful structure can represent any data model, from traditional key-value pairs to complex graph structures. Doublets provide a unified approach to data storage with constant-time lookup operations using size-balanced trees.\n\n### Key Features\n\n- **File-mapped storage** - data persists directly to disk using memory-mapped files\n- **Generic link types** - supports any unsigned integer type (`u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `usize`)\n- **Two storage modes**:\n  - `unit::Store` - combined data and index storage in a single memory region\n  - `split::Store` - separated data and index storage for optimized memory layouts\n- **Thread-safe** - `Send` and `Sync` implementations for concurrent access\n- **Query system** - flexible pattern matching using `any` constants\n- **FFI bindings** - C-compatible foreign function interface for cross-language integration\n\n## Deletion and release\n\n`delete*` methods retain automatic endpoint reset as a checked convenience.\nFor an already reset live link, `doublets::mem::Release::release` releases its\nslot without another update. `CheckedRelease` offers the same release-only\nbehavior in decorator stacks; adding `NonNullContentsLinkDeletionResolver`\nexplicitly enables resetting. An unsafe primitive is available to callers that\ncan guarantee the release contract. Incoming references remain valid in both\nlayouts, including after address reuse. See [deletion and release](docs/deletion.md)\nfor contracts, examples, callbacks and usage policies.\n\n## Checked and unchecked mutation\n\nThe safe `update*` and `delete*` methods of both stores reject a missing address\nwith `Error::NotExists`. They leave the store unchanged and make no callback.\nThat check is the explicit `decorators::CheckedMutation` adapter. A caller that\nalready guarantees a live address can omit it by calling\n`unsafe doublets::mem::UncheckedMutation::update_unchecked` and\n`Release::release_unchecked`. To ignore a missing deletion instead of returning\nan error, add `NonExistentDeletionResolver`; it never swallows unrelated errors.\nSee [checked and unchecked mutation](docs/mutation.md) for the preconditions and\nthe routes.\n\n## Installation\n\nAdd to your `Cargo.toml`:\n\n```toml\n[dependencies]\ndoublets = \"0.21.0\"\n```\n\nUse stable Rust 1.85 or newer. The repository's `rust-toolchain.toml` selects the\nstable channel, and the crate declares `rust-version = \"1.85\"` in\n`doublets/Cargo.toml`.\n\n```bash\nrustup toolchain install stable\ncargo +stable build\n```\n\nFor source checkouts, standalone FFI builds, and troubleshooting older nightly\ndependency errors, see [Stable Rust Support](STABLE_RUST.md).\n\nTo depend on the current Git source instead of a crates.io release:\n\n```toml\n[dependencies]\ndoublets = { git = \"https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs\", branch = \"main\" }\n```\n\nBoth sources build on stable Rust. If a Git dependency still reports the old\n`impl Trait` or unknown-feature errors from\n[issue 19](https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/issues/19), follow the\n[Git dependency troubleshooting steps](STABLE_RUST.md#git-dependencies-and-issue-19).\n\n## Example\n\nBasic CRUD operations with doublets:\n\n```rust\nuse doublets::{mem, unit, Doublets, DoubletsExt, Link, Links};\nuse data::Flow;\n\nfn main() -> Result<(), doublets::Error<usize>> {\n    // Use file as persistent storage for doublets\n    let mem = mem::FileMapped::from_path(\"db.links\")?;\n    let mut store = unit::Store::<usize, _>::new(mem)?;\n\n    // Create a point link (a link that references itself as both source and target)\n    // Point: 1 -> (1, 1)\n    let point = store.create_point()?;\n    println!(\"Created point: {}\", point);\n\n    // Create a regular link with explicit source and target\n    // Link: 2 -> (1, 1)\n    let link = store.create_link(point, point)?;\n    println!(\"Created link: {}\", link);\n\n    // The `any` constant matches any link in queries\n    let any = store.constants().any;\n\n    // Count all links in the store\n    println!(\"Total links: {}\", store.count());\n\n    // Iterate over all links using pattern [any, any, any]\n    println!(\"All links:\");\n    store.each_iter([any, any, any]).for_each(|link| {\n        println!(\"  {}: {} -> {}\", link.index, link.source, link.target);\n    });",

[2026-11-25T10:34:54.317Z] [INFO]     "stdout": "//! Works around a `doublets` 0.5.0 and `platform-mem` 0.3.0 mismatch: stores take the slice returned by\n//! `RawMem::grow` for their whole memory, but the memories return only the grown part. A fresh store then\n//! sees 2^20 − 8,192 = 1,040,384 links of its 2^20 and panics with \"index out of bounds\" when it creates\n//! more, and any later growth would leave it with an empty memory. [`Whole`] returns the whole memory.\n\nuse doublets::mem::{FileMapped, Global, RawMem, Result};\nuse std::{mem::MaybeUninit, path::Path};\n\npub struct Whole<M>(pub M);\n\nimpl<M: RawMem> RawMem for Whole<M> {\n    type Item = M::Item;\n\n    fn allocated(&self) -> &[Self::Item] {\n        self.0.allocated()\n    }\n\n    fn allocated_mut(&mut self) -> &mut [Self::Item] {\n        self.0.allocated_mut()\n    }\n\n    unsafe fn grow(\n        &mut self,\n        addition: usize,\n        fill: impl FnOnce(usize, (&mut [Self::Item], &mut [MaybeUninit<Self::Item>])),\n    ) -> Result<&mut [Self::Item]> {\n        // SAFETY: the caller's contract is passed on unchanged.\n        unsafe { self.0.grow(addition, fill)? };\n        Ok(self.0.allocated_mut())\n    }\n\n    fn shrink(&mut self, cap: usize) -> Result<()> {\n        self.0.shrink(cap)\n    }\n\n    fn size_hint(&self) -> Option<usize> {\n        self.0.size_hint()\n    }\n}\n\n/// Memory of the volatile stores.\npub fn volatile<T>() -> Whole<Global<T>> {\n    Whole(Global::new())\n}\n\n/// Memory of the non-volatile stores, mapped from `path`.\npub fn mapped<T>(path: impl AsRef<Path>) -> Whole<FileMapped<T>> {\n    Whole(FileMapped::from_path(path).unwrap())\n}\n\n#[cfg(test)]\nmod tests {\n    use super::*;\n\n    #[test]\n    fn grow_returns_the_whole_memory() {\n        let mut memory = Global::<u64>::new();\n        memory.grow_filled(2, 1).unwrap();\n        assert_eq!(memory.grow_filled(3, 2).unwrap(), [2, 2, 2]);\n        let mut memory = volatile::<u64>();\n        memory.grow_filled(2, 1).unwrap();\n        assert_eq!(memory.grow_filled(3, 2).unwrap(), [1, 1, 2, 2, 2]);\n No custom journal, no relaxed sync policy, no batching of the syncs — the point is to measure what a user of 0.8.0 gets when they ask the library for durability.\n\nSuggested mapping onto the existing harness:\n\n- bump `doublets` to `0.8.0`;\n- `unit::Store::<T, _>::new(mapped(dir, \"links.links\"))?.with_transactions(FileTransitionLog::open(file(dir, \"links.journal\"))?)`;\n- one Doublets transaction per lifecycle phase: `begin_transaction()` on the first write inside the phase's `transaction()` closure, `commit()` at its end. A file-backed store behaves very differently once it doesn't fit: each access to a non-resident page is a disk read, and the two engines have opposite shapes for that case — SQLite's B-tree pages hold hundreds of keys per 4 KiB page, while Doublets' index trees spread one 32/64-byte node per page touched, and its united layout interleaves both trees with the data, so the working set of any content lookup is the entire file. On GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners: `sudo systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=24M --same-dir --wait cargo run --release ... --variants SQLite_File,Doublets_United_NonVolatile`. The warm-up at 10,000 links fits inside either limit, so it stays a warm-up.\n- `--repetitions 1`. [2026-11-25T10:38:39.434Z] [INFO]     "stdout": "45 /tmp/issue127.md\nThe README says the non-volatile Doublets stores are compared with SQLite of the same durability (`SQLite File`). They are not paying for the same thing:\n\n- `SQLite File` is timed with its rollback journal and the fsyncs at every `COMMIT` (`synchronous=FULL`, stock defaults) inside the measured region.\n- `Doublets_*_NonVolatile` is a `FileMapped` store with no journal and no `msync`/`fsync` anywhere; the harness's `transaction()` for Doublets is the no-op default, and `measure()` deletes the workspace right after the run, so the data need never reach disk at all. A crash in the middle of `update` leaves SQLite consistent and the Doublets index trees torn.\n\nSo the current rows compare \"durable at commit\" with \"file-backed, no guarantee\". Since doublets 0.8.0 (2026-10-08) the library has its own answer to this — `TransactionsDecorator` with `FileTransitionLog` — and the benchmark should use it for the pairing it claims to make.\n\n## Request 1: the transactional Doublets row at 10M\n\nPlease add a Rust links variant at **10,000,000 links**, 32-bit and 64-bit, that runs the united store behind the shipped transaction layer, with **the journal exactly as shipped: `FileTransitionLog`, which calls `sync_all` after every appended record**. No custom journal, no relaxed sync policy, no batching of the syncs — the point is to measure what a user of 0.8.0 gets when they ask the library for durability.\n\nSuggested mapping onto the existing harness:\n\n- bump `doublets` to `0.8.0`;\n- `unit::Store::<T, _>::new(mapped(dir, \"links.links\"))?.with_transactions(FileTransitionLog::open(file(dir, \"links.journal\"))?)`;\n- one Doublets transaction per lifecycle phase: `begin_transaction()` on the first write inside the phase's `transaction()` closure, `commit()` at its end. Beginning lazily on the first write keeps the read-only phases free of the begin/commit snapshots the decorator persists, which is the same deal SQLite gets for a read-only `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`, so the read rows stay comparable;\n- same lifecycle, same checks, same data; `--repetitions 1` as for the other 10M tables.\n\nThen publish that row next to `SQLite File` as the same-durability comparison, and either label the plain `NonVolatile` rows as file-backed without durability guarantees or drop the \"same durability\" sentence for them.\n\nHeads-up on cost: with the shipped journal every written link is at least one fsync (two per `create_link`, since it is a create followed by an update), so the write phases at 10M are tens of millions of fsyncs. Depending on the runner's disk that may not fit in the 6-hour job limit; a local run, or the workflow's manual size input, may be needed. Please don't work around it by changing the sync policy — that is the measurement.\n\n## Request 2: SQLite's configuration\n\n`SqliteLinks::new` runs on a stock connection: `cache_size` is the 2 MiB default and `mmap_size` is 0, against a 501 MiB file at 10M. A file-backed store behaves very differently once it doesn't fit: each access to a non-resident page is a disk read, and the two engines have opposite shapes for that case — SQLite's B-tree pages hold hundreds of keys per 4 KiB page, while Doublets' index trees spread one 32/64-byte node per page touched, and its united layout interleaves both trees with the data, so the working set of any content lookup is the entire file. Please run the links lifecycle for `SQLite_File` and `Doublets_United_NonVolatile` (and the split non-volatile store) under a memory limit, at **1,000,000 and 10,000,000 links**, 32-bit, and publish them as separate tables labelled with the limit.\n\nHow:\n\n- Put the benchmark process in a cgroup with a memory limit; cgroup memory accounting charges the page cache, so the mapped store and SQLite's file pages are evicted once the limit is reached. On GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners: `sudo systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=24M --same-dir --wait cargo run --release ... --variants SQLite_File,Doublets_United_NonVolatile`. Locally, cgroup v2 `memory.max` or v1 `memory.limit_in_bytes` works the same way.\n- Limit: about 75% of the Doublets store file and 50% of the SQLite file — **24 MiB at 1M** (stores of 32 MiB and 48 MiB) and **240 MiB at 10M** (320 MiB and 501 MiB) — so neither fits, with the same ratio at both sizes. The warm-up at 10,000 links fits inside either limit, so it stays a warm-up.\n- `--repetitions 1`. Record the disk's random 4 KiB read latency in the provenance alongside the CPU, since under pressure it is the quantity being measured.\n- The transactional variant from Request 1 can't take part as is: the decorator keeps every transition and a full-graph snapshot in memory, which exceeds any limit small enough to create pressure. That is worth stating in the README as well.\n\nTime: under the limit each tree hop that misses is a disk read, so the Doublets phases take minutes at 1M and hours at 10M; the 10M table will almost certainly need a manual or local run.",

Since doublets 0.8.0 (2026-10-08) the library has its own answer to this — `TransactionsDecorator` with `FileTransitionLog` — and the benchmark should use it for the pairing it claims to make.\n\n## Request 1: the transactional Doublets row at 10M\n\nPlease add a Rust links variant at **10,000,000 links**, 32-bit and 64-bit, that runs the united store behind the shipped transaction layer, with **the journal exactly as shipped: `FileTransitionLog`, which calls `sync_all` after every appended record**. No custom journal, no relaxed sync policy, no batching of the syncs — the point is to measure what a user of 0.8.0 gets when they ask the library for durability.\n\nSuggested mapping onto the existing harness:\n\n- bump `doublets` to `0.8.0`;\n- `unit::Store::<T, _>::new(mapped(dir, \"links.links\"))?.with_transactions(FileTransitionLog::open(file(dir, \"links.journal\"))?)`;\n- one Doublets transaction per lifecycle phase: `begin_transaction()` on the first write inside the phase's `transaction()` closure, `commit()` at its end. Depending on the runner's disk that may not fit in the 6-hour job limit; a local run, or the workflow's manual size input, may be needed. A file-backed store behaves very differently once it doesn't fit: each access to a non-resident page is a disk read, and the two engines have opposite shapes for that case — SQLite's B-tree pages hold hundreds of keys per 4 KiB page, while Doublets' index trees spread one 32/64-byte node per page touched, and its united layout interleaves both trees with the data, so the working set of any content lookup is the entire file. Please run the links lifecycle for `SQLite_File` and `Doublets_United_NonVolatile` (and the split non-volatile store) under a memory limit, at **1,000,000 and 10,000,000 links**, 32-bit, and publish them as separate tables labelled with the limit.\n\nHow:\n\n- Put the benchmark process in a cgroup with a memory limit; cgroup memory accounting charges the page cache, so the mapped store and SQLite's file pages are evicted once the limit is reached. Locally, cgroup v2 `memory.max` or v1 `memory.limit_in_bytes` works the same way.\n- Limit: about 75% of the Doublets store file and 50% of the SQLite file — **24 MiB at 1M** (stores of 32 MiB and 48 MiB) and **240 MiB at 10M** (320 MiB and 501 MiB) — so neither fits, with the same ratio at both sizes. The warm-up at 10,000 links fits inside either limit, so it stays a warm-up.\n- `--repetitions 1`. SQLite\n  stores the table `blog_posts(id, title, content, publication_date)`;\n  Doublets stores every post as links, with strings as sequences of Unicode\n  symbols, like\n  [Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences](https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets.Sequences)\n  does. The operations are create, read all, read by id and delete. Every\n  Doublets store runs with and without a cache of the string sequences\n  (`Cached`/`Uncached`).\n\nStorages: SQLite in memory and in a file; Doublets united (one array of links\nwith index trees) and split (separate data and index arrays), each volatile\n(in memory) and non-volatile (in memory-mapped files). Doublets are compared\nwith SQLite of the same durability: volatile with `SQLite Memory`,\nnon-volatile with `SQLite File`.\n\nC# also runs `SystemDataSQLite_Memory` and `SystemDataSQLite_File` with\nSystem.Data.SQLite 2.0.4. `SQLite_Memory` and `SQLite_File` use\nMicrosoft.Data.Sqlite. Both providers use the same schemas, parameterized\ncommands, immediate transactions and native `e_sqlite3` library supplied by\nMicrosoft.Data.Sqlite, on Linux, macOS and Windows. The JSON reports record\neach provider and engine version in `sqlite_providers`. The System.Data.SQLite\nrows compare with Microsoft.Data.Sqlite of the same durability. Published\ntables from older runs include only the providers measured in those runs;\nthe next Benchmarks run adds the new rows.\n\nC# object benchmarks also support `PostgreSQL_EFCore` using\n[Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL](https://www.npgsql.org/efcore/).\nSet `POSTGRESQL_CONNECTION_STRING` to include it in the default object comparison;\nembedded benchmarks work without a PostgreSQL server. Explicitly selecting it\nwithout configuration fails with a setup message. Both id widths use the same\ndeterministic posts, scattered point reads, validated operations, warm-ups and\ntransaction boundaries as the other object stores. EF saves one post at a time,\nclears tracking after each save, reads without tracking and deletes by id.\nEach warm-up and repetition creates and drops its own generated schema; the\ndatabase and other schemas remain intact. The configured user needs permission\nto connect and create schemas in a benchmark database.\n\nPostgreSQL is a server database and EF Core adds ORM and network costs. Its row\nshows absolute timings without an embedded-storage speed ratio. `server_bytes`\nmeasures the benchmark table, indexes and TOAST storage after creation, shown in\na separate server-relations column; it excludes shared WAL, server memory and\nlocal client files. JSON and generated tables record PostgreSQL, Npgsql EF Core\nand EF Core versions. Existing published measurements stay intact. CI adds a\npinned PostgreSQL service to each C# object benchmark job so all compared\nvariants still run on the same machine. Set `POSTGRESQL_VERBOSE=1` to log EF\ndiagnostics to stderr; logging is off by default and sensitive values are disabled.\n\nEvery repetition runs on a fresh store in an empty directory, after discarded\nwarm-up repetitions on up to 10,000 records that run for at least a second, so\nthe .NET JIT has already optimized the code. Each operation is one\ntimed transaction over all records, point operations visit the records in a\nscattered order, and each result is checked against the expected count and\norder-sensitive checksum, so a storage that loses, duplicates or mixes up\nrecords fails the run instead of being reported as fast. Repetitions are\n`3,000,000 / size` for links and `500,000 / size` for objects, clamped to\n`1..=10`. The tables show the median time per operation; a difference is\nreported only if the interquartile ranges (the middle half) of the\nrepetitions do not overlap and the medians differ by more than 5%, otherwise\nit is `≈ same`. The file size is measured after creation; Doublets files are\npreallocated memory-mapped files, so small stores show the preallocation size.\n\nEach results group includes linear and logarithmic charts. Linear charts raise\nbars below 0.5% of the panel maximum for visibility; the tables retain exact\ntimes. Provenance records the Doublets library and Rust compiler or .NET SDK\nversions used for that run. Older reports without this metadata identify it\nas missing rather than attributing current toolchains to past measurements.\n\nEvery table is measured by its own GitHub Actions job, with all variants on\nthe same runner, so that a difference is never a difference between machines,\nby the [Benchmarks workflow](.github/workflows/benchmarks.yml): links with\n100,000, 1,000,000 and 10,000,000 records and objects with 100,000 and\n1,000,000 records. These are the largest sizes that fit into the 6 hour limit\nof a job: one SQLite File repetition on 100,000,000 links did not finish in\n4.5 hours\n([run 37228604862](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/37228604862)),\nand 1,000,000 blog posts already take an hour in C#. Pull requests check the\nwhole pipeline on 1,000 records, and pushes to `main` update the results below.\nThe workflow can also be started manually with other sizes.\n\nRun locally:\n\n```bash\nmkdir The stale entries then hide *other* links from `SearchOrDefault`. This happens in both `UnitedMemoryLinks<T>` and `SplitMemoryLinks<T>`.\n\nThe `Platform.Data.Doublets.ILinksExtensions.Delete(links, id, handler)` overload resets the link before deleting it, and it works correctly. The plain `Platform.Data.ILinksExtensions.Delete(links, id)` (`links.Delete(id)`) does not.\n\n## Minimal reproduction\n\n```csharp\nusing Platform.Data;\nusing Platform.Data.Doublets;\nusing Platform.Data.Doublets.Memory.United.Generic;\nusing Platform.Memory;\n\nforeach (var reset in new[] { false, true })\n{\n    using var links = new UnitedMemoryLinks<ulong>(new HeapResizableDirectMemory());\n    foreach (var (source, target) in new (ulong, ulong)[] { (1, 1), (2, 2), (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 3) })\n    {\n        links.CreateAndUpdate(source, target); // ids 1..5\n    }\n    if (reset)\n    {\n        Platform.Data.Doublets.ILinksExtensions.Delete(links, 4UL, null); // resets (2 1) to (0 0) first\n    }\n    else\n    {\n        links.Delete(4UL); // Platform.Data.ILinksExtensions.Delete\n    }\n    Console.WriteLine($\"{(reset ? \"Delete(4, handler: null)\" : \"Delete(4)\")}: count = {links.Count()}, \" +\n        $\"search(1, 1) = {links.SearchOrDefault(1UL, 1UL)}, search(2, 2) = {links.SearchOrDefault(2UL, 2UL)}, \" +\n        $\"search(1, 2) = {links.SearchOrDefault(1UL, 2UL)}, search(2, 3) = {links.SearchOrDefault(2UL, 3UL)}\");\n}\n```\n\nOutput (net10.0, Platform.Data.Doublets 1.0.0):\n\n```\nDelete(4): count = 4, search(1, 1) = 1, search(2, 2) = 0, search(1, 2) = 3, search(2, 3) = 0\nDelete(4, handler: null): count = 4, search(1, 1) = 1, search(2, 2) = 2, search(1, 2) = 3, search(2, 3) = 5\n```\n\n**Expected:** after deleting link 4 `(2 1)`, `search(2, 2) = 2` and `search(2, 3) = 5`.\n**Actual:** both return `0`, even though links 2 and 5 still exist.\n\nA randomized version is in [experiments/csharp_tree_delete](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/tree/issue-127-8556896db129/experiments/csharp_tree_delete). It creates random stores and deletes every unreferenced link. Without the reset, the united store fails at 7 links and the split store at 13. With the reset, neither fails up to 151 links. Platform.Data.Doublets 0.18.1 gives the same results.\n\n## Expected behaviour\n\nThe memory stores' `Delete` should detach the link from the source and target trees itself, the way `Update` does, so that every `Delete` overload leaves the indexes consistent.\n\n## Workaround used downstream\n\n[Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets) deletes through `Platform.Data.Doublets.ILinksExtensions.Delete(links, id, handler: null)`.\nEOF\ncat > trees.md <<'EOF'\n## Summary\n\nWith Platform.Data.Doublets 1.0.0, the default (size-balanced) index trees of `UnitedMemoryLinks<T>` degenerate when thousands of links share one source or target. Updating a link onto such a shared source then becomes about 10× slower as the store grows. `IndexTreeType.SizedAndThreadedAVLBalancedTree` does not have this problem, and neither does the split store.\n\n## Reproduction\n\n[experiments/csharp_objects_profile](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/tree/issue-127-8556896db129/experiments/csharp_objects_profile) stores 10,000 blog posts as doublets. Each post is attached to a type marker by `Update(link, marker, link)`, so every post shares that marker as its source. A counting decorator times each `ILinks` call. The table shows the mean time of that one update for posts 1..1,000 versus posts 9,001..10,000 (`dotnet run -c Release -- united 10000 <tree type>`):\n\n| Store / index tree | posts 1..1,000 | posts 9,001..10,000 |\n|---|---|---|\n| united `Default` | 20 µs | 184 µs |\n| united `SizeBalancedTree` | 25 µs | 335 µs |\n| united `RecursionlessSizeBalancedTree` | 22 µs | 275 µs |\n| united `SizedAndThreadedAVLBalancedTree` | 27 µs | 2.0 µs |\n| split (default) | 1.0 µs | 0.2 µs |\n\nOther updates that attach links to frequently shared markers grow in the same way with the size-balanced trees. For example, `Update[link,marker4]` goes from 23 µs to 293 µs with `Default` and from 27 µs to 2.7 µs with AVL. All other calls stay flat. Platform.Data.Doublets 0.18.1 showed the same pattern (`Default`: 27 µs → 322 µs).\n\n## Expected behaviour\n\nThe cost of attaching a link to a source should stay roughly logarithmic in the number of links sharing that source, whichever tree type is used. Alternatively, the default index tree type of the united store could be the AVL tree.\n\n## Workaround used downstream\n\n[Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets) constructs `UnitedMemoryLinks<T>` with `IndexTreeType.SizedAndThreadedAVLBalancedTree`.\nEOF\ngh issue create --repo linksplatform/Data.Doublets --title \"C#: Delete(id) without a reset leaves stale index tree entries that hide other links from SearchOrDefault\" --body-file delete.md; gh issue create --repo linksplatform/Data.Doublets --title \"C#: united store size-balanced index trees degenerate when many links share a source\" --body-file trees.md"

[2026-11-25T10:55:45.709Z] [INFO]       "command": "mkdir -p /tmp/issue_bodies && cd /tmp/issue_bodies && cat > delete.md <<'EOF'\n## Summary\n\nWith Platform.Data.Doublets 1.0.0, deleting a link via `ILinks<T>.Delete(restriction, handler)` without first resetting it to `(0, 0)` frees the link but leaves it in the source and target index trees. The stale entries then hide *other* links from `SearchOrDefault`. This happens in both `UnitedMemoryLinks<T>` and `SplitMemoryLinks<T>`.\n\nThe `Platform.Data.Doublets.ILinksExtensions.Delete(links, id, handler)` overload resets the link before deleting it, and it works correctly. The plain `Platform.Data.ILinksExtensions.Delete(links, id)` (`links.Delete(id)`) does not.\n\n## Minimal reproduction\n\n```csharp\nusing Platform.Data;\nusing Platform.Data.Doublets;\nusing Platform.Data.Doublets.Memory.United.Generic;\nusing Platform.Memory;\n\nforeach (var reset in new[] { false, true })\n{\n    using var links = new UnitedMemoryLinks<ulong>(new HeapResizableDirectMemory());\n    foreach (var (source, target) in new (ulong, ulong)[] { (1, 1), (2, 2), (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 3) })\n    {\n        links.CreateAndUpdate(source, target); // ids 1..5\n    }\n    if (reset)\n    {\n        Platform.Data.Doublets.ILinksExtensions.Delete(links, 4UL, null); // resets (2 1) to (0 0) first\n    }\n    else\n    {\n        links.Delete(4UL); // Platform.Data.ILinksExtensions.Delete\n    }\n    Console.WriteLine($\"{(reset ? \"Delete(4, handler: null)\" : \"Delete(4)\")}: count = {links.Count()}, \" +\n        $\"search(1, 1) = {links.SearchOrDefault(1UL, 1UL)}, search(2, 2) = {links.SearchOrDefault(2UL, 2UL)}, \" +\n        $\"search(1, 2) = {links.SearchOrDefault(1UL, 2UL)}, search(2, 3) = {links.SearchOrDefault(2UL, 3UL)}\");\n}\n```\n\nOutput (net10.0, Platform.Data.Doublets 1.0.0):\n\n```\nDelete(4): count = 4, search(1, 1) = 1, search(2, 2) = 0, search(1, 2) = 3, search(2, 3) = 0\nDelete(4, handler: null): count = 4, search(1, 1) = 1, search(2, 2) = 2, search(1, 2) = 3, search(2, 3) = 5\n```\n\n**Expected:** after deleting link 4 `(2 1)`, `search(2, 2) = 2` and `search(2, 3) = 5`.\n**Actual:** both return `0`, even though links 2 and 5 still exist.\n\nA randomized version is in [experiments/csharp_tree_delete](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/tree/issue-127-8556896db129/experiments/csharp_tree_delete). It creates random stores and deletes every unreferenced link. Without the reset, the united store fails at 7 links and the split store at 13. With the reset, neither fails up to 151 links. Platform.Data.Doublets 0.18.1 gives the same results.\n\n## Expected behaviour\n\nThe memory stores' `Delete` should detach the link from the source and target trees itself, the way `Update` does, so that every `Delete` overload leaves the indexes consistent.\n\n## Workaround used downstream\n\n[Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets) deletes through `Platform.Data.Doublets.ILinksExtensions.Delete(links, id, handler: null)`.\nEOF\ncat > trees.md <<'EOF'\n## Summary\n\nWith Platform.Data.Doublets 1.0.0, the default (size-balanced) index trees of `UnitedMemoryLinks<T>` degenerate when thousands of links share one source or target. Updating a link onto such a shared source then becomes about 10× slower as the store grows. `IndexTreeType.SizedAndThreadedAVLBalancedTree` does not have this problem, and neither does the split store.\n\n## Reproduction\n\n[experiments/csharp_objects_profile](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/tree/issue-127-8556896db129/experiments/csharp_objects_profile) stores 10,000 blog posts as doublets. Each post is attached to a type marker by `Update(link, marker, link)`, so every post shares that marker as its source. A counting decorator times each `ILinks` call. The table shows the mean time of that one update for posts 1..1,000 versus posts 9,001..10,000 (`dotnet run -c Release -- united 10000 <tree type>`):\n\n| Store / index tree | posts 1..1,000 | posts 9,001..10,000 |\n|---|---|---|\n| united `Default` | 20 µs | 184 µs |\n| united `SizeBalancedTree` | 25 µs | 335 µs |\n| united `RecursionlessSizeBalancedTree` | 22 µs | 275 µs |\n| united `SizedAndThreadedAVLBalancedTree` | 27 µs | 2.0 µs |\n| split (default) | 1.0 µs | 0.2 µs |\n\nOther updates that attach links to frequently shared markers grow in the same way with the size-balanced trees. For example, `Update[link,marker4]` goes from 23 µs to 293 µs with `Default` and from 27 µs to 2.7 µs with AVL. All other calls stay flat. Platform.Data.Doublets 0.18.1 showed the same pattern (`Default`: 27 µs → 322 µs).\n\n## Expected behaviour\n\nThe cost of attaching a link to a source should stay roughly logarithmic in the number of links sharing that source, whichever tree type is used. Alternatively, the default index tree type of the united store could be the AVL tree.\n\n## Workaround used downstream\n\n[Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets) constructs `UnitedMemoryLinks<T>` with `IndexTreeType.SizedAndThreadedAVLBalancedTree`.\nEOF\ngh issue create --repo linksplatform/Data.Doublets --title \"C#: Delete(id) without a reset leaves stale index tree entries that hide other links from SearchOrDefault\" --body-file delete.md; gh issue create --repo linksplatform/Data.Doublets --title \"C#: united store size-balanced index trees degenerate when many links share a source\" --body-file trees.md"

Record the disk's random 4 KiB read latency in the provenance alongside the CPU, since under pressure it is the quantity being measured.\n- The transactional variant from Request 1 can't take part as is: the decorator keeps every transition and a full-graph snapshot in memory, which exceeds any limit small enough to create pressure. That is worth stating in the README as well.\n\nTime: under the limit each tree hop that misses is a disk read, so the Doublets phases take minutes at 1M and hours at 10M; the 10M table will almost certainly need a manual or local run.",

C#\n([Platform.Data.Doublets](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Platform.Data.Doublets),\n[Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences)\nand the providers [Microsoft.Data.Sqlite](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.Data.Sqlite)\nand [System.Data.SQLite](https://www.nuget.org/packages/System.Data.SQLite))\nrun the same workloads on the same deterministic data, with 32 bit\n(`u32`/`uint`) and 64 bit (`u64`/`ulong`) ids:\n\n\nЗамечания:\n\n- Разделённые хранилища doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) теряют связь, обновлённую так,\n  чтобы она ссылалась на саму себя, поэтому тест сначала обновляет связь\n  до `(0, 0)` — состояния, в котором связи создаются\n  ([experiments/split_store_delete](experiments/split_store_delete)).\n- Хранилища doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) принимают часть памяти, которую\n  `platform-mem` 0.3.0 возвращает после её увеличения, за всю память, поэтому\n  хранилище ломается после 1 040 384 связей; тесты оборачивают память\n  в [`memory::Whole`](rust/src/memory.rs), которая возвращает всю память\n  ([experiments/unit_store_growth](experiments/unit_store_growth)).\n- В C# связи удаляются через `Delete(id, handler: null)`, который сбрасывает\n  связь перед удалением; простой `Delete(id)` оставляет связь в деревьях\n  индексов, и последующий поиск ломается\n  ([experiments/csharp_tree_delete](experiments/csharp_tree_delete)).\n- Объединённые хранилища на C# используют АВЛ-деревья индексов: деревья\n  по умолчанию, сбалансированные по размеру, вырождаются, ([experiments/csharp_objects_profile](experiments/csharp_objects_profile)).\n- Раздельные хранилища на C# оставляют связный список внутренних начал,\n  который включён по умолчанию и которого нет в doublets 0.5.0 (Rust); с ним\n  обновления на C# быстрее, а остальные операции занимают примерно то же время\n  ([experiments/csharp_split_linked_list](experiments/csharp_split_linked_list)).\n- Хранилища объектов используют внешние ссылки для чисел и символов Юникода,\n  поэтому исходные значения никогда не совпадают с идентификаторами связей.\n- Чтение строки без кэша обходит её последовательность связь за связью; в C#\n  каждый вызов `GetSource`/`GetTarget` из `Platform.Data` выделяет обработчик\n  и список, поэтому чтение без кэша на C# значительно медленнее, чем на of models](https://github.com/LinksPlatform/Documentation/raw/master/doc/ModelsComparison/relational_model_vs_associative_model_vs_links.png)\n\nComparison of SQLite and LinksPlatform's Doublets (links) on basic embedded\ndatabase operations with links and object-like structures.\n\nBased on examples from <https://github.com/FahaoTang/dotnetcore-examples> and\n<https://github.com/Konard/LinksPlatform>\n\n## Benchmarks\n\nRust ([doublets](https://crates.io/crates/doublets) and\n[rusqlite](https://crates.io/crates/rusqlite) with bundled SQLite) and C#\n([Platform.Data.Doublets](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Platform.Data.Doublets),\n[Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences)\nand the providers [Microsoft.Data.Sqlite](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.Data.Sqlite)\nand [System.Data.SQLite](https://www.nuget.org/packages/System.Data.SQLite))\nrun the same workloads on the same deterministic data, with 32 bit\n(`u32`/`uint`) and 64 bit (`u64`/`ulong`) ids:\n\n- **Links**: SQLite stores the table\n  `links(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, \"from\", \"to\")` with the indices\n  `(\"from\", \"to\")` and `(\"to\", \"from\")`; Doublets stores the links themselves.\n  The operations are create, read all, read by id, search by `(from, to)`,\n  read by `from`, read by `to`, update (swap `from` and `to`) and delete.\n- **Objects**: blog posts with a title, content and publication date. SQLite\n  stores the table `blog_posts(id, title, content, publication_date)`;\n  Doublets stores every post as links, with strings as sequences of Unicode\n  symbols, like\n  [Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences](https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets.Sequences)\n  does. The operations are create, read all, read by id and delete. Every\n  Doublets store runs with and without a cache of the string sequences\n  (`Cached`/`Uncached`).\n\nStorages: SQLite in memory and in a file; Doublets united (one array of links\nwith index trees) and split (separate data and index arrays), each volatile\n(in memory) and non-volatile (in memory-mapped files). Doublets stores the links themselves.\n  The operations are create, read all, read by id, search by `(from, to)`,\n  read by `from`, read by `to`, update (swap `from` and `to`) and delete.\n- **Objects**: blog posts with a title, content and publication date. SQLite\n  stores the table `blog_posts(id, title, content, publication_date)`;\n  Doublets stores every post as links, with strings as sequences of Unicode\n  symbols, like\n  [Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences](https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets.Sequences)\n  does. The operations are create, read all, read by id and delete. Every\n  Doublets store runs with and without a cache of the string sequences\n  (`Cached`/`Uncached`).\n\nStorages: SQLite in memory and in a file; Doublets united (one array of links\nwith index trees) and split (separate data and index arrays), each volatile\n(in memory) and non-volatile (in memory-mapped files). Doublets are compared\nwith SQLite of the same durability: volatile with `SQLite Memory`,\nnon-volatile with `SQLite File`.\n\nC# also runs `SystemDataSQLite_Memory` and `SystemDataSQLite_File` with\nSystem.Data.SQLite 2.0.4. `SQLite_Memory` and `SQLite_File` use\nMicrosoft.Data.Sqlite. Both providers use the same schemas, parameterized\ncommands, immediate transactions and native `e_sqlite3` library supplied by\nMicrosoft.Data.Sqlite, on Linux, macOS and Windows. The JSON reports record\neach provider and engine version in `sqlite_providers`. The System.Data.SQLite\nrows compare with Microsoft.Data.Sqlite of the same durability. Published\ntables from older runs include only the providers measured in those runs;\nthe next Benchmarks run adds the new rows.\n\nC# object benchmarks also support `PostgreSQL_EFCore` using\n[Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL](https://www.npgsql.org/efcore/).\nSet `POSTGRESQL_CONNECTION_STRING` to include it in the default object comparison;\nembedded benchmarks work without a PostgreSQL server. Explicitly selecting it\nwithout configuration fails with a setup message. Both id widths use the same\ndeterministic posts, scattered point reads, validated operations, warm-ups and\ntransaction boundaries as the other object stores. EF saves one post at a time,\nclears tracking after each save, reads without tracking and deletes by id.\nEach warm-up and repetition creates and drops its own generated schema; the\ndatabase and other schemas remain intact. The configured user needs permission\nto connect and create schemas in a benchmark database.\n\nPostgreSQL is a server database and EF Core adds ORM and network costs. Its row\nshows absolute timings without an embedded-storage speed ratio. `server_bytes`\nmeasures the benchmark table, indexes and TOAST storage after creation, shown in\na separate server-relations column; it excludes shared WAL, server memory and\nlocal client files. JSON and generated tables record PostgreSQL, Npgsql EF Core\nand EF Core versions. Existing published measurements stay intact. CI adds a\npinned PostgreSQL service to each C# object benchmark job so all compared\nvariants still run on the same machine. Set `POSTGRESQL_VERBOSE=1` to log EF\ndiagnostics to stderr; logging is off by default and sensitive values are disabled.\n\nEvery repetition runs on a fresh store in an empty directory, after discarded\nwarm-up repetitions on up to 10,000 records that run for at least a second, so\nthe .NET JIT has already optimized the code. Each operation is one\ntimed transaction over all records, point operations visit the records in a\nscattered order, and each result is checked against the expected count and\norder-sensitive checksum, so a storage that loses, duplicates or mixes up\nrecords fails the run instead of being reported as fast. Repetitions are\n`3,000,000 / size` for links and `500,000 / size` for objects, clamped to\n`1..=10`. The tables show the median time per operation; a difference is\nreported only if the interquartile ranges (the middle half) of the\nrepetitions do not overlap and the medians differ by more than 5%, otherwise\nit is `≈ same`. The file size is measured after creation; Doublets files are\npreallocated memory-mapped files, so small stores show the preallocation size.\n\nEach results group includes linear and logarithmic charts. Linear charts raise\nbars below 0.5% of the panel maximum for visibility; the tables retain exact\ntimes. Provenance records the Doublets library and Rust compiler or .NET SDK\nversions used for that run. Older reports without this metadata identify it\nas missing rather than attributing current toolchains to past measurements.\n\nEvery table is measured by its own GitHub Actions job, with all variants on\nthe same runner, so that a difference is never a difference between machines,\nby the [Benchmarks workflow](.github/workflows/benchmarks.yml): links with\n100,000, 1,000,000 and 10,000,000 records and objects with 100,000 and\n1,000,000 records. These are the largest sizes that fit into the 6 hour limit\nof a job: one SQLite File repetition on 100,000,000 links did not finish in\n4.5 hours\n([run 37228604862](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/37228604862)),\nand 1,000,000 blog posts already take an hour in C#. Pull requests check the\nwhole pipeline on 1,000 records, and pushes to `main` update the results below.\nThe workflow can also be started manually with other sizes.\n\nRun locally:\n\n```bash\nmkdir -p results\ncargo run --release --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -- \\\n  links 64 100000 --output results/links-rust-64-100000.json\ndotnet run -c Release --project csharp/SQLiteVSDoublets -- \\\n  objects 32 1000 --variants SQLite_File,Doublets_Split_NonVolatile_Cached\ndotnet run -c Release --project csharp/SQLiteVSDoublets -- \\\n  links 64 1000 --repetitions 3 \\\n  --variants SQLite_Memory,SystemDataSQLite_Memory \\\n  --output results/links-csharp-64-1000.json\npython3 scripts/benchmark_provenance.py results/links-rust-64-100000.json \\\n  --toolchain \"$(rustc --version)\"\npython3 scripts/benchmark_provenance.py results/links-csharp-64-1000.json \\\n  --toolchain \".NET SDK $(dotnet --version)\"\n# print the tables, add --readme README.md --charts docs/benchmarks to update\npython3 scripts/benchmark_report.py results\n```\n\nRun a bounded PostgreSQL comparison:\n\n```bash\ndocker run -d --name benchmark-postgres -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 \\\n  -e POSTGRES_USER=benchmark -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=[REDACTED] \\\n  -e POSTGRES_DB=benchmark postgres:18.3\nexport POSTGRESQL_CONNECTION_STRING='Host=127.0.0.1;Database=benchmark;Username=benchmark;Password=[REDACTED]'\ndotnet run -c Release --project csharp/SQLiteVSDoublets -- \\\n  objects 64 1000 --repetitions 3 \\\n  --variants SQLite_Memory,SQLite_File,PostgreSQL_EFCore \\\n  --output results/objects-csharp-64-1000.json\npython3 scripts/benchmark_report.py results\npython3 experiments/postgresql/check_reports.py\ndocker stop benchmark-postgres\ndocker rm benchmark-postgres\n```\n\nNotes:\n\n- The split stores of doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) lose a link that is updated to\n  reference itself, so the benchmark updates a link to `(0, 0)` first, which\n  is the state links are created in\n  ([experiments/split_store_delete](experiments/split_store_delete)).\n- The stores of doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) take the part of the memory that\n  `platform-mem` 0.3.0 returns after growing it for the whole memory, so a\n  store fails after 1,040,384 links; the benchmarks wrap the memory in\n  [`memory::Whole`](rust/src/memory.rs), which returns the whole memory\n  ([experiments/unit_store_growth](experiments/unit_store_growth)).\n- In C#, links are deleted with `Delete(id, handler: null)`, which resets the\n  link before deleting it; the bare `Delete(id)` leaves the link in the index\n  trees, and later searches fail\n  ([experiments/csharp_tree_delete](experiments/csharp_tree_delete)).\n- The C# united stores use AVL index trees: the default size balanced trees\n  degenerate when many links share a source or a target, which makes each\n  blog post creation linear in the number of posts\n  ([experiments/csharp_objects_profile](experiments/csharp_objects_profile)).\n- The C# split stores keep the default linked list of the internal sources,\n  which doublets 0.5.0 (Rust) does not have; it makes the C# updates faster\n  and the other operations take about the same time\n  ([experiments/csharp_split_linked_list](experiments/csharp_split_linked_list)).\n- Objects stores use external references for numbers and Unicode symbols, so\n  raw values never collide with link ids.\n- Reading a string without the cache walks its sequence link by link; in C#\n  each `GetSource`/`GetTarget` call of `Platform.Data` allocates a handler and\n  a list, which makes the uncached C# reads much slower than the Rust ones.",

Each\nlifecycle phase that writes is one transaction, begun at its first write and\ncommitted at its end. The\ngenerated section below shows them as separate tables after the regular\nresults:\n\n- **Durable file storage**, 10,000,000 links, 32 and 64 bit:\n  `SQLite File`, `SQLite File Tuned` and\n  `Doublets United NonVolatile Transactional`.\n- **Under memory pressure**, 32 bit: `SQLite File`,\n  `Doublets United NonVolatile` and `Doublets Split NonVolatile` in a cgroup\n  with `memory.max` of 24 MiB at 1,000,000 links and 240 MiB at 10,000,000\n  links, without swap. The limit charges the page cache too, so the stores'\n  pages are read back from the disk. The warm-up on 10,000 links fits in\n  either limit. The table records the cgroup's `memory.peak` and major page\n  faults. `SQLite File Tuned` is left out, because its 1 GiB cache would be\n  anonymous memory charged to the limit. The transactional store can't take\n  part: its decorator keeps every transition and a full snapshot of the links\n  in memory, which no limit small enough to create pressure can hold.\n\nBoth kinds record the disk the stores use: the median latency of a random\n4 KiB read that bypasses the page cache (`O_DIRECT`) and of an `fsync` after\na small append. Pull requests run the pipeline on a small plan (1,000 durable\nlinks and 20,000 links under 24 MiB); the published tables come from a run\nwith the plan above.
