The libraries are bumped to their latest releases, and the bugs in them that stand in the way of the closest comparison are reported upstream, each with a workaround in this repository.\n\nFixes #127.\n\n## Changes\n\n**Request 1: the transactional Doublets row at 10M**\n\n- `Doublets_United_NonVolatile_Transactional` (Rust, opt-in `links` variant) puts the united file-mapped store behind doublets' `TransactionsDecorator`, with the shipped `FileTransitionLog`, which calls `sync_all` after every record.\n- The journal policy is left exactly as shipped. That is 32 MiB of dirty pages per growth of a 32-bit united store, so the 24 MiB run was OOM-killed before its first measured link.\n  - Workaround: `rust/src/memory.rs` `ZeroExtended` reports the extension as initialized, so the reservation stays a hole.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/issues/94: the split store's linked list of internal sources (`USE_LIST`) is unimplemented (`todo!()`). The Rust split store uses trees, unlike the C# default, and the READMEs say so.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets/issues/576: C# `Delete(id)` without a reset leaves stale index entries.\n  - Workaround: the harness still calls `Delete(id, handler: null)`. `experiments/csharp_delete_minimal` and `experiments/csharp_tree_delete` reproduce the bug on 1.0.0.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets/issues/577: the united store's size-balanced trees degenerate when many links share a source. It is documented, and the C# united store uses the AVL trees.\n\n## Memory-limit OOM root causes\n\nThe 24 MiB job was killed twice, for two different reasons. The kernel stats are in the job logs.\n\n1. **Zero-filled reservation** (doublets-rs#95 above): the reservation was written over with zeros. Fixed by `ZeroExtended`.\n   - `mapped_stores_do_not_write_their_reservation_and_reopen_with_their_links` checks on Linux that the reservation stays unallocated and that the store reopens with its links.\n   - On APFS the extension is allocated anyway (macOS 15, run 45603348935), so the check runs on Linux only, where the memory-limit runs happen.\n2. **Dirty page thresholds computed from the whole runner**, in run 45604850024:\n   - The united store dirtied 21 MiB of its mapping (15 MiB under writeback) before writeback throttled it, and memcg reclaim failed: `oom_kill 1`.\n   - The kernel's `dirty_ratio` (20%) and `dirty_background_ratio` (10%) apply to the 16 GiB runner, not to the cgroup.\n   - The memory-limit jobs now set `vm.dirty_bytes` and `vm.dirty_background_bytes` to 20% and 10% of the limit, as on a machine with that much memory. This applies to every variant, and the values are recorded in the report and shown in the tables. SQLite is unaffected, because it syncs every commit.\n   - RESULT_PLACEHOLDER\n\n## Reproduction and regression coverage\n\n- Rust (`rust/tests/storages.rs`):\n  - `every_optional_links_variant_passes_the_lifecycle` runs the tuned and transactional variants through the checked lifecycle.\n  - `transactional_store_commits_one_transaction_per_written_phase` and `transactional_store_journals_writes_outside_a_phase_one_by_one` read the journal entries.\n  - `mapped_stores_keep_their_links_when_their_memory_grows` and the reservation test above cover growth.\n- C# (`StoragesTests.cs`): `SQLiteVariantsAreRegistered` and `TunedSQLiteFilesApplyThePragmas` read the pragmas back from both providers.\n- Python (`scripts/test_benchmark_configuration.py`, `scripts/test_benchmark_report.py`) covers:\n  - plan validation, the disk probe, cgroup stats parsing and recording, including the dirty thresholds, which are refused for a durable report;\n  - rejection of invalid configured reports (the transactional store under a limit, a missing limit or latency, invalid thresholds);\n  - the rendered sections in both languages;\n  - an exact match between the committed READMEs and the generator.\n\nRun the configured benchmarks locally as described in README \"Configured benchmarks\". [2026-11-25T12:11:24.277Z] [INFO]       "content": "The non-volatile Doublets rows were labelled as comparisons with SQLite of the same durability. `SQLite File` fsyncs its rollback journal and database at every `COMMIT`, while the mapped Doublets stores have no journal and never sync. This change measures the durable pairing the README claimed and gives SQLite a configuration that matches a fully mapped store. It also adds tables for the file-backed stores under memory pressure. The libraries are bumped to their latest releases, and the bugs in them that stand in the way of the closest comparison are reported upstream, each with a workaround in this repository.\n\nFixes #127.\n\n## Changes\n\n**Request 1: the transactional Doublets row at 10M**\n\n- `Doublets_United_NonVolatile_Transactional` (Rust, opt-in `links` variant) puts the united file-mapped store behind doublets' `TransactionsDecorator`, with the shipped `FileTransitionLog`, which calls `sync_all` after every record.\n- The journal policy is left exactly as shipped. Each lifecycle phase that writes is one transaction: it begins at the phase's first write and commits at the phase's end, so the read phases begin none.\n- It is published next to `SQLite File` (stock defaults, `synchronous=FULL`) in a new \"Durable file storage\" section at 10,000,000 links, 32 and 64 bit, with `--repetitions 1`.\n- The plain `NonVolatile` rows are now described as \"file-backed without durability guarantees\" in both READMEs.\n\n**Request 2: SQLite's configuration**\n\n- A new `SQLite File Tuned` row runs `PRAGMA cache_size = -1048576; PRAGMA mmap_size = 1073741824;` before the schema is created.\n- It exists in Rust (`SQLite_File_Tuned`) and in both C# providers (`SQLite_File_Tuned` on Microsoft.Data.Sqlite, `SystemDataSQLite_File_Tuned` on System.Data.SQLite).\n- The file-backed Doublets rows are compared with it wherever it was measured.\n\n**Request 3: memory pressure**\n\n- `SQLite_File`, `Doublets_United_NonVolatile` and `Doublets_Split_NonVolatile` (32 bit) run inside a `systemd-run --scope` with `MemoryMax`, `MemorySwapMax=0` and `--repetitions 1`:\n  - 24 MiB at 1,000,000 links;\n  - 240 MiB at 10,000,000 links.\n- They are published as separate tables labelled with the limit. The provenance line records the cgroup's `memory.peak`, the major page faults and the dirty page thresholds.\n- Both configured kinds record the disk the stores use: the median `O_DIRECT` random 4 KiB read latency and the `fsync` latency.\n- The READMEs state that the transactional store cannot take part, because its decorator keeps every transition and a full snapshot of the links in memory. The report validation rejects a memory-limit report that contains it.\n\n**Pipeline**\n\n- `.github/workflows/configurations.yml` plans and runs the configured jobs.\n- `scripts/benchmark_configuration.py` provides `plan`, `probe`, `record` and `report`. The configured reports are kept in `docs/benchmarks/configurations` and validated separately from the default reports, and the README sections are generated from them.\n- Pull requests run a small smoke plan. The published tables come from a run of the full plan on this pull request (see Validation).\n\n**Latest dependencies**\n\n| Dependency | Version |\n| --- | --- |\n| doublets (Rust) | 0.21.0 |\n| platform-mem | 0.4.0 |\n| rusqlite | 0.43.0, bundling SQLite 3.54.1 |\n| Platform.Data.Doublets | 1.0.0 |\n| Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences | 0.6.5 |\n| Microsoft.Data.Sqlite | 11.0.0, bundling SQLite 3.53.4 |\n| System.Data.SQLite | 2.0.4 |\n\n- doublets 0.21.0 fixes the 0.5.0 growth and split self-reference bugs, so those workarounds are removed. `experiments/unit_store_growth` and `experiments/split_store_delete` pass on it.\n- `Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL` 11.0.0 targets only `net11.0`, according to its NuGet catalog entry, so it stays at 10.0.3 on `net10.0`.\n- `link-cli` and `links-notation` are not used by this repository, so there is nothing to bump.\n- The Rust and C# tables use different SQLite engine versions (3.54.1 and 3.53.4), as bundled by their providers. The provenance lines record both.\n\n## Upstream bugs reported, with the workarounds kept here\n\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/issues/95: file-backed stores write zeros over every reservation, because `grow_filled` runs over a `set_len` extension. That is 32 MiB of dirty pages per growth of a 32-bit united store, so the 24 MiB run was OOM-killed before its first measured link.\n  - Workaround: `rust/src/memory.rs` `ZeroExtended` reports the extension as initialized, so the reservation stays a hole.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/issues/94: the split store's linked list of internal sources (`USE_LIST`) is unimplemented (`todo!()`). The Rust split store uses trees, unlike the C# default, and the READMEs say so.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets/issues/576: C# `Delete(id)` without a reset leaves stale index entries.\n  - Workaround: the harness still calls `Delete(id, handler: null)`. `experiments/csharp_delete_minimal` and `experiments/csharp_tree_delete` reproduce the bug on 1.0.0.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets/issues/577: the united store's size-balanced trees degenerate when many links share a source. It is documented, and the C# united store uses the AVL trees.\n\n## Memory-limit OOM root causes\n\nThe 24 MiB job was killed twice, for two different reasons. The kernel stats are in the job logs.\n\n1. **Zero-filled reservation** (doublets-rs#95 above): the reservation was written over with zeros. Fixed by `ZeroExtended`.\n   - `mapped_stores_do_not_write_their_reservation_and_reopen_with_their_links` checks on Linux that the reservation stays unallocated and that the store reopens with its links.\n   - On APFS the extension is allocated anyway (macOS 15, run 45603348935), so the check runs on Linux only, where the memory-limit runs happen.\n2. **Dirty page thresholds computed from the whole runner**, in run 45604850024:\n   - The united store dirtied 21 MiB of its mapping (15 MiB under writeback) before writeback throttled it, and memcg reclaim failed: `oom_kill 1`.\n   - The kernel's `dirty_ratio` (20%) and `dirty_background_ratio` (10%) apply to the 16 GiB runner, not to the cgroup.\n   - The memory-limit jobs now set `vm.dirty_bytes` and `vm.dirty_background_bytes` to 20% and 10% of the limit, as on a machine with that much memory. This applies to every variant, and the values are recorded in the report and shown in the tables. SQLite is unaffected, because it syncs every commit.\n   - RESULT_PLACEHOLDER\n\n## Reproduction and regression coverage\n\n- Rust (`rust/tests/storages.rs`):\n  - `every_optional_links_variant_passes_the_lifecycle` runs the tuned and transactional variants through the checked lifecycle.\n  - `transactional_store_commits_one_transaction_per_written_phase` and `transactional_store_journals_writes_outside_a_phase_one_by_one` read the journal entries.\n  - `mapped_stores_keep_their_links_when_their_memory_grows` and the reservation test above cover growth.\n- C# (`StoragesTests.cs`): `SQLiteVariantsAreRegistered` and `TunedSQLiteFilesApplyThePragmas` read the pragmas back from both providers.\n- Python (`scripts/test_benchmark_configuration.py`, `scripts/test_benchmark_report.py`) covers:\n  - plan validation, the disk probe, cgroup stats parsing and recording, including the dirty thresholds, which are refused for a durable report;\n  - rejection of invalid configured reports (the transactional store under a limit, a missing limit or latency, invalid thresholds);\n  - the rendered sections in both languages;\n  - an exact match between the committed READMEs and the generator.\n\nRun the configured benchmarks locally as described in README \"Configured benchmarks\". Volatile Doublets are\n+compared with `SQLite Memory`. Non-volatile Doublets are file-backed without\n+durability guarantees: they write no journal and never call `fsync`, so a\n+crash can lose or corrupt any write since the operating system last flushed\n+the mapped pages. `SQLite File` keeps its defaults (a rollback journal and\n+`synchronous=FULL`) and syncs at every commit, so it is durable at commit.\n+\n+`SQLite File Tuned` is the same file with the pragmas\n+`PRAGMA cache_size = -1048576; PRAGMA mmap_size = 1073741824;` run before the\n+schema: a 1 GiB page cache instead of the default 2 MiB and reads through a\n+1 GiB memory map, like the Doublets stores read their mapped files. Its\n+durability is unchanged. Rust and both C# providers run it\n+(`SQLite_File_Tuned` and `SystemDataSQLite_File_Tuned`), and the summary\n+compares the non-volatile Doublets with it.\n+\n+`Doublets United NonVolatile Transactional` (Rust) is the united file-mapped\n+store behind doublets' `TransactionsDecorator` with the shipped\n+`FileTransitionLog`, which calls `sync_all` after every journal record. Each\n+lifecycle phase that writes is one transaction, begun at its first write and\n+committed at its end. It is durable at commit like `SQLite File`, and it is\n+measured in its own table, see [Configured benchmarks](#configured-benchmarks).\n+### Configured benchmarks\n+\n+The [Configured benchmarks workflow](.github/workflows/configurations.yml)\n+measures Rust links tables in a non-default setup, each table in its own job\n+with `--repetitions 1`, and stores them in\n+[docs/benchmarks/configurations](docs/benchmarks/configurations). The configured-benchmarks path checks out: the Rust code is unchanged since the published durable tables were measured (their `tree_sha` is commit 4caf6c2's tree), regenerating both README sections from `docs/benchmarks/{results,configurations}` gives exactly what is committed, and the 85 script unit tests pass.\n\n### Findings\n\n**1. The dirty-page thresholds are much stricter than the README and provenance say.** `.github/workflows/configurations.yml:105-106` (medium confidence on the kernel behaviour, lower on how much it changes timings)\n- The workflow sets the global `vm.dirty_bytes` to 20% of the limit (and `vm.dirty_background_bytes` to 10%). The README says this is \"as on a machine with that much memory\", and provenance prints \"Dirty page cache limit 4.8 MiB\".\n- But in `mm/page-writeback.c` (`domain_dirty_limits`), byte settings are not applied to a cgroup directly. The kernel converts them to a ratio of the whole machine's dirtyable memory and then applies that ratio to the cgroup's own memory.\n- Worked through for 24 MiB on a 16 GiB runner: 4.8 MiB ÷ ~15 GiB rounds up to 2/4096. The cgroup's threshold then comes to about 3 pages (~12 KiB), and the background threshold to about 1–2 pages.\n- So the mapped Doublets stores are probably being throttled almost every page. Measurements would be taken under a much harsher regime than recorded, and the published \"4.8 MiB\" would be wrong. The default ratios already give the cgroup about 20% of its own memory, so the earlier OOM may have had another cause (the global rate limit, for example).\n- How to check: compare `file_dirty`/`file_writeback` in the captured `memory.stat`, or one timing, with and without the sysctl. Nothing under a memory limit is published yet, so this affects future tables and the README text.\n\n**2. A bad plan doesn't fail the Plan step.** `.github/workflows/configurations.yml:47` (high confidence, low impact)\n- In `echo \"matrix=$(python ... plan \"$PLAN\")\"`, the shell ignores a failure inside `$(...)`, so the step writes `matrix=` and succeeds.\n- The run still fails, but later and less clearly: the benchmark job errors on `fromJSON('')` instead of showing the plan's `ValueError`. Assigning the output to a variable first would surface the real error.\n\n**3. The README's local example runs `benchmark_report.py results --configurations results/configured`.** (low)\n- `load()` only reads `results/*.json` and raises \"No benchmark reports found\" unless default reports are already in `results/`. That is fine if you already have them; on a clean checkout it fails as written.\n\n### Checked and found correct\n- **Transactional variant (`rust/src/links.rs`):** a transaction starts on a phase's first write and commits inside the timed closure. Read-only phases write nothing to the journal. A panic rolls back when the transaction is dropped. Writes outside a phase are committed one at a time by the doublets library itself. The README's durability claim is accurate: `FileTransitionLog` fsyncs every record, and each commit writes a full snapshot. The reported file size includes the journal (about 2 GB at 10M links).\n- **`ZeroExtended`:** reporting the whole new region as already initialized is safe here. `FileMapped` (platform-mem 0.4.0) extends the file with `set_len`, which reads as zeros, and every store directory starts empty.\n- **Tuned SQLite pragmas:** rusqlite 0.43's `execute_batch` accepts `PRAGMA mmap_size` returning a row (the check is compiled out). C# connections have pooling off, so the per-connection pragmas can't leak into other variants.\n- **Report merging (`merge_jobs`/`load_configurations`):** jobs from different runs are rejected because `run_url` and `source_sha` must match, duplicate storages are rejected, and a merged table must include SQLite File. The variant comparisons fall back to `SQLite_File` when there is no tuned row.\n- **Workflow shell:** the quoting of the `systemd-run`/`sh -c` call and its arguments, the exit-status propagation, and the `chown` order are correct. The `memory.events` keys can't collide with `pgmajfault` in `cgroup_stats`."

[2026-11-25T18:25:08.983Z] [INFO]         "content": "\"Same durability\" comparison: run Doublets 0.8.0 behind its own transaction journal (fsync per write) against SQLite File at 10M, and add a memory-pressure configuration\nThe README says the non-volatile Doublets stores are compared with SQLite of the same durability (`SQLite File`). They are not paying for the same thing:\n\n- `SQLite File` is timed with its rollback journal and the fsyncs at every `COMMIT` (`synchronous=FULL`, stock defaults) inside the measured region.\n- `Doublets_*_NonVolatile` is a `FileMapped` store with no journal and no `msync`/`fsync` anywhere; the harness's `transaction()` for Doublets is the no-op default, and `measure()` deletes the workspace right after the run, so the data need never reach disk at all. A crash in the middle of `update` leaves SQLite consistent and the Doublets index trees torn.\n\nSo the current rows compare \"durable at commit\" with \"file-backed, no guarantee\". Since doublets 0.8.0 (2026-10-08) the library has its own answer to this — `TransactionsDecorator` with `FileTransitionLog` — and the benchmark should use it for the pairing it claims to make.\n\n## Request 1: the transactional Doublets row at 10M\n\nPlease add a Rust links variant at **10,000,000 links**, 32-bit and 64-bit, that runs the united store behind the shipped transaction layer, with **the journal exactly as shipped: `FileTransitionLog`, which calls `sync_all` after every appended record**. No custom journal, no relaxed sync policy, no batching of the syncs — the point is to measure what a user of 0.8.0 gets when they ask the library for durability.\n\nSuggested mapping onto the existing harness:\n\n- bump `doublets` to `0.8.0`;\n- `unit::Store::<T, _>::new(mapped(dir, \"links.links\"))?.with_transactions(FileTransitionLog::open(file(dir, \"links.journal\"))?)`;\n- one Doublets transaction per lifecycle phase: `begin_transaction()` on the first write inside the phase's `transaction()` closure, `commit()` at its end. Beginning lazily on the first write keeps the read-only phases free of the begin/commit snapshots the decorator persists, which is the same deal SQLite gets for a read-only `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`, so the read rows stay comparable;\n- same lifecycle, same checks, same data; `--repetitions 1` as for the other 10M tables.\n\nThen publish that row next to `SQLite File` as the same-durability comparison, and either label the plain `NonVolatile` rows as file-backed without durability guarantees or drop the \"same durability\" sentence for them.\n\nHeads-up on cost: with the shipped journal every written link is at least one fsync (two per `create_link`, since it is a create followed by an update), so the write phases at 10M are tens of millions of fsyncs. Depending on the runner's disk that may not fit in the 6-hour job limit; a local run, or the workflow's manual size input, may be needed. Please don't work around it by changing the sync policy — that is the measurement.\n\n## Request 2: SQLite's configuration\n\n`SqliteLinks::new` runs on a stock connection: `cache_size` is the 2 MiB default and `mmap_size` is 0, against a 501 MiB file at 10M. The Doublets file-backed store is, by construction, the whole file mapped into memory, so the matching SQLite configuration is\n\n```rust\nconnection.execute_batch(\"PRAGMA cache_size = -1048576; PRAGMA mmap_size = 1073741824;\").unwrap();\n```\n\nbefore the schema is created (and the equivalent pragmas for the two C# providers). Please add a tuned `SQLite File` row, or make this the default for the File variants, so the SQLite side is not measured through a 2 MiB cache.\n\n## Request 3: a memory-pressure configuration, 1M and 10M\n\nEvery published table measures stores that fit in RAM (the largest file is 800 MiB on a 16 GiB runner). A file-backed store behaves very differently once it doesn't fit: each access to a non-resident page is a disk read, and the two engines have opposite shapes for that case — SQLite's B-tree pages hold hundreds of keys per 4 KiB page, while Doublets' index trees spread one 32/64-byte node per page touched, and its united layout interleaves both trees with the data, so the working set of any content lookup is the entire file. Please run the links lifecycle for `SQLite_File` and `Doublets_United_NonVolatile` (and the split non-volatile store) under a memory limit, at **1,000,000 and 10,000,000 links**, 32-bit, and publish them as separate tables labelled with the limit.\n\nHow:\n\n- Put the benchmark process in a cgroup with a memory limit; cgroup memory accounting charges the page cache, so the mapped store and SQLite's file pages are evicted once the limit is reached. On GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners: `sudo systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=24M --same-dir --wait cargo run --release ... --variants SQLite_File,Doublets_United_NonVolatile`. With the kernel's default dirty page thresholds, a mapped store's dirty pages and pages under writeback filled the limit, which reclaim cannot free, and the store was killed. So the runner's `vm.dirty_bytes` and `vm.dirty_background_bytes` are set to 20% and 10% of the limit. The kernel applies byte thresholds to a cgroup as a fraction of the runner's whole memory, rounded up to 1/4096, of the memory the cgroup can use, so the cgroup's own thresholds are a few pages under 24 MiB and below 1 MiB under 240 MiB: the mapped stores write back their pages almost as soon as they dirty them. Under pressure a store can take hours, so each storage runs in its own job of one run, and the second table shows each job's runner, disk latencies, peak cgroup memory and major page faults. [2026-11-25T19:49:19.346Z] [INFO]                 " `Doublets United NonVolatile Transactional` — объединённое хранилище в отображаемом файле за `TransactionsDecorator` из doublets с поставляемым `FileTransitionLog`, который вызывает `sync_all` после каждой записи журнала. Оно сравнивается с `SQLite File`, который синхронизирует журнал отката и базу при каждом `COMMIT` (`synchronous=FULL`): оба надёжны при фиксации."

[2026-11-25T19:49:52.128Z] [INFO]                 " ## Durable file storage",
[2026-11-25T19:49:52.128Z] [INFO]                 " ",
[2026-11-25T19:49:52.128Z] [INFO]                 " `Doublets United NonVolatile Transactional` is the united file-mapped store behind doublets' `TransactionsDecorator` with the shipped `FileTransitionLog`, which calls `sync_all` after every journal record. One transaction covers each lifecycle phase that writes: it begins at the phase's first write and commits at its end, so the read phases begin none. It is compared with `SQLite File`, which syncs its rollback journal and database at every `COMMIT` (`synchronous=FULL`): both are durable at commit."

Convert them to ratios by scaling against globally available memory.\"). It then applies that ratio to the memory the cgroup can use, so under 24 MiB the cgroup's thresholds came to a few pages. Earlier commits of this PR described the byte values as the cgroup's thresholds, which was wrong.\n   - Ratios alone: `balance_dirty_pages` compares the cgroup's dirty and writeback pages with its thresholds using `mem_cgroup_wb_stats`. That function reads the memcg counters after `mem_cgroup_flush_stats_ratelimited` (`mm/memcontrol.c`), and the counters are flushed every 2 s (`FLUSH_TIME`). In that window the united store, at about a microsecond per link, dirtied the whole limit. Reclaim cannot free pages under writeback, so the charge failed. This explanation comes from the kernel sources (v6.11) and the stats above, not from a kernel trace: the runners don't allow tracing the cgroup's charges.\n   - `memory.high`: a task above it reclaims and sleeps on its way back to user space (`mem_cgroup_handle_over_high`), which gives the writeback time to finish before `memory.max`. The limit stays `memory.max`, and `memory.high` is recorded in the report and shown in the provenance line.\n\n'''\ns=s[:a]+new+s[b:]\ns=s.replace(\"The provenance line shows the dirty page thresholds.\",\"The provenance line shows `memory.high` and the dirty page thresholds.\")\nopen(p,'w').write(s)\nEOF\ngrep -n 'PLACEHOLDER' /tmp/pr179/body.md"

The provenance lines record both.\n\n## Upstream bugs reported, with the workarounds kept here\n\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/issues/95: file-backed stores write zeros over every reservation, because `grow_filled` runs over a `set_len` extension. That is 32 MiB of dirty pages per growth of a 32-bit united store, so the 24 MiB run was OOM-killed before its first measured link.\n  - Workaround: `rust/src/memory.rs` `ZeroExtended` reports the extension as initialized, so the reservation stays a hole.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/issues/94: the split store's linked list of internal sources (`USE_LIST`) is unimplemented (`todo!()`). The Rust split store uses trees, unlike the C# default, and the READMEs say so.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets/issues/576: C# `Delete(id)` without a reset leaves stale index entries.\n  - Workaround: the harness still calls `Delete(id, handler: null)`. `experiments/csharp_delete_minimal` and `experiments/csharp_tree_delete` reproduce the bug on 1.0.0.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets/issues/577: the united store's size-balanced trees degenerate when many links share a source. It is documented, and the C# united store uses the AVL trees.\n\n## Memory-limit OOM root causes\n\nThe 24 MiB job was killed twice, for two different reasons. The kernel stats are in the job logs.\n\n1. **Zero-filled reservation** (doublets-rs#95 above): the reservation was written over with zeros. Fixed by `ZeroExtended`.\n   - `mapped_stores_do_not_write_their_reservation_and_reopen_with_their_links` checks on Linux that the reservation stays unallocated and that the store reopens with its links.\n   - On APFS the extension is allocated anyway (macOS 15, run 45603348935), so the check runs on Linux only, where the memory-limit runs happen.\n2. **Dirty and writeback pages that reclaim cannot free.** Each setting below was tried in a dispatch of the 24 MiB, 1M-link table. The job logs have the scope samples and the final `memory.stat` and `memory.events`.\n\n   | Setting | Run | Outcome |\n   | --- | --- | --- |\n   | Kernel defaults, `vm.dirty_ratio` 20%, `vm.dirty_background_ratio` 10% | [45604850024](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45604850024) | United store killed (`oom_kill 1`): 21.6 MiB of file pages, all dirty, 15.7 MiB under writeback. |\n   | `vm.dirty_bytes` and `vm.dirty_background_bytes` at 20% and 10% of the limit | [45681559798](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45681559798) | Every store, SQLite too, waited in `balance_dirty_pages` with I/O pressure and no memory pressure. |\n   | `vm.dirty_ratio` 5%, `vm.dirty_background_ratio` 2% | [45683252380](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45683252380) | SQLite and the split store run under real memory pressure (read waits, major faults). The united store was killed 4 s into `create`: 23.3 MiB of file pages, all under writeback. |\n   | The same, plus `strict_limit` on the storage disk's bdi | [45685437372](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45685437372) | No kill, but the mapped stores were throttled in `balance_dirty_pages` to about 3 MiB of file pages in 6 minutes, with no memory pressure. |\n   | The same ratios, plus `memory.high` at 7/8 of the limit (kept) | [45687063141](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45687063141) | No kill (`max 0`, `oom_kill 0`), peak at most 21.8 MiB. All three stores run under memory pressure: the united store had 448,638 major faults in 6 minutes. |\n\n   - Byte thresholds: for a cgroup, `domain_dirty_limits` in `mm/page-writeback.c` converts byte thresholds into a ratio of the runner's available memory, rounded up to 1/4096 (\"The byte settings can't be applied directly to memcg domains. Convert them to ratios by scaling against globally available memory.\"). It then applies that ratio to the memory the cgroup can use, so under 24 MiB the cgroup's thresholds came to a few pages. Earlier commits of this PR described the byte values as the cgroup's thresholds, which was wrong.\n   - Ratios alone: `balance_dirty_pages` compares the cgroup's dirty and writeback pages with its thresholds using `mem_cgroup_wb_stats`. That function reads the memcg counters after `mem_cgroup_flush_stats_ratelimited` (`mm/memcontrol.c`), and the counters are flushed every 2 s (`FLUSH_TIME`). In that window the united store, at about a microsecond per link, dirtied the whole limit. Reclaim cannot free pages under writeback, so the charge failed. This explanation comes from the kernel sources (v6.11) and the stats above. It was not confirmed with a kernel trace.\n   - `memory.high`: a task above it reclaims and sleeps on its way back to user space (`mem_cgroup_handle_over_high`), which gives the writeback time to finish before `memory.max`. The limit stays `memory.max`, and `memory.high` is recorded in the report and shown in the provenance line.\n\n## Reproduction and regression coverage\n\n- Rust (`rust/tests/storages.rs`):\n  - `every_optional_links_variant_passes_the_lifecycle` runs the tuned and transactional variants through the checked lifecycle.\n  - `transactional_store_commits_one_transaction_per_written_phase` and `transactional_store_journals_writes_outside_a_phase_one_by_one` read the journal entries.\n  - `mapped_stores_keep_their_links_when_their_memory_grows` and the reservation test above cover growth.\n- C# (`StoragesTests.cs`): `SQLiteVariantsAreRegistered` and `TunedSQLiteFilesApplyThePragmas` read the pragmas back from both providers.\n- Python (`scripts/test_benchmark_configuration.py`, `scripts/test_benchmark_report.py`) covers:\n  - plan validation, with one job per storage under a limit, the disk probe, cgroup stats parsing and recording, including the dirty thresholds, which are refused for a durable report;\n  - merging the per-storage reports of one table in the configured order, and refusing reports from different runs, duplicated storages, a table without `SQLite File` and duplicated durable reports;\n  - rejection of invalid configured reports (the transactional store under a limit, a missing limit or latency, invalid thresholds);\n  - the rendered sections in both languages;\n  - an exact match between the committed READMEs and the generator.\n\nRun the configured benchmarks locally as described in README \"Configured benchmarks\". The report validation rejects a memory-limit report that contains it.\n\n**Pipeline**\n\n- `.github/workflows/configurations.yml` plans and runs the configured jobs.\n- `scripts/benchmark_configuration.py` provides `plan`, `probe`, `record` and `report`. The configured reports are kept in `docs/benchmarks/configurations` and validated separately from the default reports, and the README sections are generated from them.\n- Pull requests run a small smoke plan. The published tables come from a run of the full plan on this pull request (see Validation).\n\n**Latest dependencies**\n\n| Dependency | Version |\n| --- | --- |\n| doublets (Rust) | 0.21.0 |\n| platform-mem | 0.4.0 |\n| rusqlite | 0.43.0, bundling SQLite 3.54.1 |\n| Platform.Data.Doublets | 1.0.0 |\n| Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences | 0.6.5 |\n| Microsoft.Data.Sqlite | 11.0.0, bundling SQLite 3.53.4 |\n| System.Data.SQLite | 2.0.4 |\n\n- doublets 0.21.0 fixes the 0.5.0 growth and split self-reference bugs, so those workarounds are removed. `experiments/unit_store_growth` and `experiments/split_store_delete` pass on it.\n- `Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL` 11.0.0 targets only `net11.0`, according to its NuGet catalog entry, so it stays at 10.0.3 on `net10.0`.\n- `link-cli` and `links-notation` are not used by this repository, so there is nothing to bump.\n- The Rust and C# tables use different SQLite engine versions (3.54.1 and 3.53.4), as bundled by their providers. The provenance lines record both.\n\n## Upstream bugs reported, with the workarounds kept here\n\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/issues/95: file-backed stores write zeros over every reservation, because `grow_filled` runs over a `set_len` extension. That is 32 MiB of dirty pages per growth of a 32-bit united store, so the 24 MiB run was OOM-killed before its first measured link.\n  - Workaround: `rust/src/memory.rs` `ZeroExtended` reports the extension as initialized, so the reservation stays a hole.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/issues/94: the split store's linked list of internal sources (`USE_LIST`) is unimplemented (`todo!()`). The Rust split store uses trees, unlike the C# default, and the READMEs say so.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets/issues/576: C# `Delete(id)` without a reset leaves stale index entries.\n  - Workaround: the harness still calls `Delete(id, handler: null)`. `experiments/csharp_delete_minimal` and `experiments/csharp_tree_delete` reproduce the bug on 1.0.0.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets/issues/577: the united store's size-balanced trees degenerate when many links share a source. It is documented, and the C# united store uses the AVL trees.\n\n## Memory-limit OOM root causes\n\nThe 24 MiB job was killed twice, for two different reasons. The kernel stats are in the job logs.\n\n1. **Zero-filled reservation** (doublets-rs#95 above): the reservation was written over with zeros. Fixed by `ZeroExtended`.\n   - `mapped_stores_do_not_write_their_reservation_and_reopen_with_their_links` checks on Linux that the reservation stays unallocated and that the store reopens with its links.\n   - On APFS the extension is allocated anyway (macOS 15, run 45603348935), so the check runs on Linux only, where the memory-limit runs happen.\n2. **Dirty and writeback pages that reclaim cannot free.** Each setting below was tried in a dispatch of the 24 MiB, 1M-link table. The job logs have the scope samples and the final `memory.stat` and `memory.events`.\n\n   | Setting | Run | Outcome |\n   | --- | --- | --- |\n   | Kernel defaults, `vm.dirty_ratio` 20%, `vm.dirty_background_ratio` 10% | [45604850024](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45604850024) | United store killed (`oom_kill 1`): 21.6 MiB of file pages, all dirty, 15.7 MiB under writeback. |\n   | `vm.dirty_bytes` and `vm.dirty_background_bytes` at 20% and 10% of the limit | [45681559798](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45681559798) | Every store, SQLite too, waited in `balance_dirty_pages` with I/O pressure and no memory pressure. |\n   | `vm.dirty_ratio` 5%, `vm.dirty_background_ratio` 2% | [45683252380](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45683252380) | SQLite and the split store run under real memory pressure (read waits, major faults). The united store was killed 4 s into `create`: 23.3 MiB of file pages, all under writeback. |\n   | The same, plus `strict_limit` on the storage disk's bdi | [45685437372](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45685437372) | No kill, but the mapped stores were throttled in `balance_dirty_pages` to about 3 MiB of file pages in 6 minutes, with no memory pressure. |\n   | The same ratios, plus `memory.high` at 7/8 of the limit (kept) | [45687063141](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45687063141) | No kill (`max 0`, `oom_kill 0`), peak at most 21.8 MiB. All three stores run under memory pressure: the united store had 448,638 major faults in 6 minutes. |\n\n   - Byte thresholds: for a cgroup, `domain_dirty_limits` in `mm/page-writeback.c` converts byte thresholds into a ratio of the runner's available memory, rounded up to 1/4096 (\"The byte settings can't be applied directly to memcg domains. Convert them to ratios by scaling against globally available memory.\"). It then applies that ratio to the memory the cgroup can use, so under 24 MiB the cgroup's thresholds came to a few pages. Earlier commits of this PR described the byte values as the cgroup's thresholds, which was wrong.\n   - Ratios alone: `balance_dirty_pages` compares the cgroup's dirty and writeback pages with its thresholds using `mem_cgroup_wb_stats`. That function reads the memcg counters after `mem_cgroup_flush_stats_ratelimited` (`mm/memcontrol.c`), and the counters are flushed every 2 s (`FLUSH_TIME`). In that window the united store, at about a microsecond per link, dirtied the whole limit. Reclaim cannot free pages under writeback, so the charge failed. This explanation comes from the kernel sources (v6.11) and the stats above. It was not confirmed with a kernel trace.\n   - `memory.high`: a task above it reclaims and sleeps on its way back to user space (`mem_cgroup_handle_over_high`), which gives the writeback time to finish before `memory.max`. The limit stays `memory.max`, and `memory.high` is recorded in the report and shown in the provenance line.\n\n## Reproduction and regression coverage\n\n- Rust (`rust/tests/storages.rs`):\n  - `every_optional_links_variant_passes_the_lifecycle` runs the tuned and transactional variants through the checked lifecycle.\n  - `transactional_store_commits_one_transaction_per_written_phase` and `transactional_store_journals_writes_outside_a_phase_one_by_one` read the journal entries.\n  - `mapped_stores_keep_their_links_when_their_memory_grows` and the reservation test above cover growth.\n- C# (`StoragesTests.cs`): `SQLiteVariantsAreRegistered` and `TunedSQLiteFilesApplyThePragmas` read the pragmas back from both providers.\n- Python (`scripts/test_benchmark_configuration.py`, `scripts/test_benchmark_report.py`) covers:\n  - plan validation, with one job per storage under a limit, the disk probe, cgroup stats parsing and recording, including the dirty thresholds, which are refused for a durable report;\n  - merging the per-storage reports of one table in the configured order, and refusing reports from different runs, duplicated storages, a table without `SQLite File` and duplicated durable reports;\n  - rejection of invalid configured reports (the transactional store under a limit, a missing limit or latency, invalid thresholds);\n  - the rendered sections in both languages;\n  - an exact match between the committed READMEs and the generator.\n\nRun the configured benchmarks locally as described in README \"Configured benchmarks\". For a cgroup, `domain_dirty_limits` in `mm/page-writeback.c` converts byte thresholds into a ratio of the runner's available memory, rounded up to 1/4096 (\"The byte settings can't be applied directly to memcg domains. On a 16 GiB runner the cgroup's own thresholds therefore come to a few pages under 24 MiB and below 1 MiB under 240 MiB, so the mapped stores write back their pages almost as soon as they dirty them. The READMEs describe it this way. One transaction covers each lifecycle phase that writes: it begins at the phase's first write and commits at its end, so the read phases begin none. It is compared with `SQLite File`, which syncs its rollback journal and database at every `COMMIT` (`synchronous=FULL`): both are durable at commit.\n\n### Rust, 32 bit, 10,000,000 links\n\n_1 repetition after a warm-up, median time per operation. This change measures the durable pairing the README claimed and gives SQLite a configuration that matches a fully mapped store. It also adds tables for the file-backed stores under memory pressure. The libraries are bumped to their latest releases, and the bugs in them that stand in the way of the closest comparison are reported upstream, each with a workaround in this repository.\n\nFixes #127.\n\n## Changes\n\n**Request 1: the transactional Doublets row at 10M**\n\n- `Doublets_United_NonVolatile_Transactional` (Rust, opt-in `links` variant) puts the united file-mapped store behind doublets' `TransactionsDecorator`, with the shipped `FileTransitionLog`, which calls `sync_all` after every record.\n- The journal policy is left exactly as shipped. Each lifecycle phase that writes is one transaction: it begins at the phase's first write and commits at the phase's end, so the read phases begin none.\n- It is published next to `SQLite File` (stock defaults, `synchronous=FULL`) in a new \"Durable file storage\" section at 10,000,000 links, 32 and 64 bit, with `--repetitions 1`.\n- The plain `NonVolatile` rows are now described as \"file-backed without durability guarantees\" in both READMEs.\n\n**Request 2: SQLite's configuration**\n\n- A new `SQLite File Tuned` row runs `PRAGMA cache_size = -1048576; PRAGMA mmap_size = 1073741824;` before the schema is created.\n- It exists in Rust (`SQLite_File_Tuned`) and in both C# providers (`SQLite_File_Tuned` on Microsoft.Data.Sqlite, `SystemDataSQLite_File_Tuned` on System.Data.SQLite).\n- The file-backed Doublets rows are compared with it wherever it was measured.\n\n**Request 3: memory pressure**\n\n- `SQLite_File`, `Doublets_United_NonVolatile` and `Doublets_Split_NonVolatile` (32 bit) run inside a `systemd-run --scope` with `MemoryMax`, `MemorySwapMax=0` and `--repetitions 1`:\n  - 24 MiB at 1,000,000 links;\n  - 240 MiB at 10,000,000 links.\n- Under pressure a store can take hours, so each storage runs in its own job of one run. [2026-11-26T01:34:51.999Z] [INFO]         "content": "total 24\n-rw-r--r-- 1 box box 1865 Nov 26 01:34 memory-limit-240MiB-links-rust-32-10000000-doublets-split-nonvolatile.json\n-rw-r--r-- 1 box box 1233 Nov 26 01:34 memory-limit-240MiB-links-rust-32-10000000-doublets-united-nonvolatile.json\n-rw-r--r-- 1 box box 2740 Nov 26 01:34 memory-limit-240MiB-links-rust-32-10000000-sqlite-file.json\n-rw-r--r-- 1 box box 2669 Nov 26 01:34 memory-limit-24MiB-links-rust-32-1000000-doublets-split-nonvolatile.json\n-rw-r--r-- 1 box box 2475 Nov 26 01:34 memory-limit-24MiB-links-rust-32-1000000-doublets-united-nonvolatile.json\n-rw-r--r-- 1 box box 2687 Nov 26 01:34 memory-limit-24MiB-links-rust-32-1000000-sqlite-file.json\nsource_sha 326f6e14f9fd4619fb41abeb7a7cb535992c4d26\n/tmp/flat-BBxNsl\n## Under memory pressure\n\nThe benchmark process runs in a cgroup with a memory limit (`memory.max`, swap disabled). The limit charges the page cache too, so neither the SQLite file nor the mapped Doublets store fits in memory, and pages that are not resident are read from the disk. With the kernel's default dirty page thresholds, a mapped store's dirty pages and pages under writeback filled the limit, which reclaim cannot free, and the store was killed. Byte thresholds do not help: the kernel applies them to a cgroup as a fraction of the runner's whole memory, rounded up to 1/4096, so 20% of the limit came to a few pages, and every store, SQLite too, waited in `balance_dirty_pages` for most of the pages it wrote. So the runner's `vm.dirty_ratio` and `vm.dirty_background_ratio` are lowered, which the kernel applies to the memory the cgroup can use. That alone did not save the united store: the kernel compares the cgroup's dirty pages with its thresholds by counts it refreshes every two seconds, and in that time the store filled the limit. So `memory.high` is set to 7/8 of the limit: a store above it reclaims and waits on its way back to user space, which gives the writeback time to finish before `memory.max`. The transactional store cannot take part: its decorator keeps every transition and a full snapshot of the links in memory, which exceeds any limit small enough to create pressure. Under pressure a store can take hours, so each storage runs in its own job of one run, and the second table shows each job's runner, disk latencies, peak cgroup memory and major page faults. Major page faults count the misses of the mapped stores only: SQLite reads its file with `read`, whose misses are not page faults.\n\n### Rust, 32 bit, 1,000,000 links, memory limit 24 MiB\n\n_1 repetition after a warm-up, median time per operation. The limit charges the page cache too, so neither the SQLite file nor the mapped Doublets store fits in memory, and pages that are not resident are read from the disk. With the kernel's default dirty page thresholds, a mapped store's dirty pages and pages under writeback filled the limit, which reclaim cannot free, and the store was killed. Byte thresholds do not help: the kernel applies them to a cgroup as a fraction of the runner's whole memory, rounded up to 1/4096, so 20% of the limit came to a few pages, and every store, SQLite too, waited in `balance_dirty_pages` for most of the pages it wrote. So the runner's `vm.dirty_ratio` and `vm.dirty_background_ratio` are lowered, which the kernel applies to the memory the cgroup can use. That alone did not save the united store: the kernel compares the cgroup's dirty pages with its thresholds by counts it refreshes every two seconds, and in that time the store filled the limit. So `memory.high` is set to 7/8 of the limit: a store above it reclaims and waits on its way back to user space, which gives the writeback time to finish before `memory.max`. The transactional store cannot take part: its decorator keeps every transition and a full snapshot of the links in memory, which exceeds any limit small enough to create pressure. Under pressure a store can take hours, so each storage runs in its own job of one run, and the second table shows each job's runner, disk latencies, peak cgroup memory and major page faults. Major page faults count the misses of the mapped stores only: SQLite reads its file with `read`, whose misses are not page faults.\n\n### Rust, 32 bit, 1,000,000 links, memory limit 24 MiB\n\n_1 repetition after a warm-up, median time per operation. The limit charges the page cache too, so neither the SQLite file nor the mapped Doublets store fits in memory, and pages that are not resident are read from the disk. With the kernel's default dirty page thresholds, a mapped store's dirty pages and pages under writeback filled the limit, which reclaim cannot free, and the store was killed. Byte thresholds do not help: the kernel applies them to a cgroup as a fraction of the runner's whole memory, rounded up to 1/4096, so 20% of the limit came to a few pages, and every store, SQLite too, waited in `balance_dirty_pages` for most of the pages it wrote. So the runner's `vm.dirty_ratio` and `vm.dirty_background_ratio` are lowered, which the kernel applies to the memory the cgroup can use. That alone did not save the united store: the kernel compares the cgroup's dirty pages with its thresholds by counts it refreshes every two seconds, and in that time the store filled the limit. So `memory.high` is set to 7/8 of the limit: a store above it reclaims and waits on its way back to user space, which gives the writeback time to finish before `memory.max`. The transactional store cannot take part: its decorator keeps every transition and a full snapshot of the links in memory, which exceeds any limit small enough to create pressure. Under pressure a store can take hours, so each storage runs in its own job of one run, and the second table shows each job's runner, disk latencies, peak cgroup memory and major page faults. Major page faults count the misses of the mapped stores only: SQLite reads its file with `read`, whose misses are not page faults.\n+\n+### Rust, 32 bit, 1,000,000 links, memory limit 24 MiB\n+\n+_1 repetition after a warm-up, median time per operation. README says the non-volatile Doublets stores are compared with SQLite of the same durability (`SQLite File`). They are not paying for the same thing:\n\n- `SQLite File` is timed with its rollback journal and the fsyncs at every `COMMIT` (`synchronous=FULL`, stock defaults) inside the measured region.\n- `Doublets_*_NonVolatile` is a `FileMapped` store with no journal and no `msync`/`fsync` anywhere; the harness's `transaction()` for Doublets is the no-op default, and `measure()` deletes the workspace right after the run, so the data need never reach disk at all. A crash in the middle of `update` leaves SQLite consistent and the Doublets index trees torn.\n\nSo the current rows compare \"durable at commit\" with \"file-backed, no guarantee\". Since doublets 0.8.0 (2026-10-08) the library has its own answer to this — `TransactionsDecorator` with `FileTransitionLog` — and the benchmark should use it for the pairing it claims to make.\n\n## Request 1: the transactional Doublets row at 10M\n\nPlease add a Rust links variant at **10,000,000 links**, 32-bit and 64-bit, that runs the united store behind the shipped transaction layer, with **the journal exactly as shipped: `FileTransitionLog`, which calls `sync_all` after every appended record**. No custom journal, no relaxed sync policy, no batching of the syncs — the point is to measure what a user of 0.8.0 gets when they ask the library for durability.\n\nSuggested mapping onto the existing harness:\n\n- bump `doublets` to `0.8.0`;\n- `unit::Store::<T, _>::new(mapped(dir, \"links.links\"))?.with_transactions(FileTransitionLog::open(file(dir, \"links.journal\"))?)`;\n- one Doublets transaction per lifecycle phase: `begin_transaction()` on the first write inside the phase's `transaction()` closure, `commit()` at its end. Beginning lazily on the first write keeps the read-only phases free of the begin/commit snapshots the decorator persists, which is the same deal SQLite gets for a read-only `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`, so the read rows stay comparable;\n- same lifecycle, same checks, same data; `--repetitions 1` as for the other 10M tables.\n\nThen publish that row next to `SQLite File` as the same-durability comparison, and either label the plain `NonVolatile` rows as file-backed without durability guarantees or drop the \"same durability\" sentence for them.\n\nHeads-up on cost: with the shipped journal every written link is at least one fsync (two per `create_link`, since it is a create followed by an update), so the write phases at 10M are tens of millions of fsyncs. Depending on the runner's disk that may not fit in the 6-hour job limit; a local run, or the workflow's manual size input, may be needed. Please don't work around it by changing the sync policy — that is the measurement.\n\n## Request 2: SQLite's configuration\n\n`SqliteLinks::new` runs on a stock connection: `cache_size` is the 2 MiB default and `mmap_size` is 0, against a 501 MiB file at 10M. The Doublets file-backed store is, by construction, the whole file mapped into memory, so the matching SQLite configuration is\n\n```rust\nconnection.execute_batch(\"PRAGMA cache_size = -1048576; PRAGMA mmap_size = 1073741824;\").unwrap();\n```\n\nbefore the schema is created (and the equivalent pragmas for the two C# providers). Please add a tuned `SQLite File` row, or make this the default for the File variants, so the SQLite side is not measured through a 2 MiB cache.\n\n## Request 3: a memory-pressure configuration, 1M and 10M\n\nEvery published table measures stores that fit in RAM (the largest file is 800 MiB on a 16 GiB runner). A file-backed store behaves very differently once it doesn't fit: each access to a non-resident page is a disk read, and the two engines have opposite shapes for that case — SQLite's B-tree pages hold hundreds of keys per 4 KiB page, while Doublets' index trees spread one 32/64-byte node per page touched, and its united layout interleaves both trees with the data, so the working set of any content lookup is the entire file. Please run the links lifecycle for `SQLite_File` and `Doublets_United_NonVolatile` (and the split non-volatile store) under a memory limit, at **1,000,000 and 10,000,000 links**, 32-bit, and publish them as separate tables labelled with the limit.\n\nHow:\n\n- Put the benchmark process in a cgroup with a memory limit; cgroup memory accounting charges the page cache, so the mapped store and SQLite's file pages are evicted once the limit is reached. On GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners: `sudo systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=24M --same-dir --wait cargo run --release ... --variants SQLite_File,Doublets_United_NonVolatile`. Locally, cgroup v2 `memory.max` or v1 `memory.limit_in_bytes` works the same way.\n- Limit: about 75% of the Doublets store file and 50% of the SQLite file — **24 MiB at 1M** (stores of 32 MiB and 48 MiB) and **240 MiB at 10M** (320 MiB and 501 MiB) — so neither fits, with the same ratio at both sizes. The warm-up at 10,000 links fits inside either limit, so it stays a warm-up.\n- `--repetitions 1`. Record the disk's random 4 KiB read latency in the provenance alongside the CPU, since under pressure it is the quantity being measured.\n- The transactional variant from Request 1 can't take part as is: the decorator keeps every transition and a full-graph snapshot in memory, which exceeds any limit small enough to create pressure. That is worth stating in the README as well.\n\nTime: under the limit each tree hop that misses is a disk read, so the Doublets phases take minutes at 1M and hours at 10M; the 10M table will almost certainly need a manual or local non-volatile Doublets rows were labelled as comparisons with SQLite of the same durability. `SQLite File` fsyncs its rollback journal and database at every `COMMIT`, while the mapped Doublets stores have no journal and never sync. This change measures the durable pairing the README claimed and gives SQLite a configuration that matches a fully mapped store. It also adds tables for the file-backed stores under memory pressure. The libraries are bumped to their latest releases, and the bugs in them that stand in the way of the closest comparison are reported upstream, each with a workaround in this repository.\n\nFixes #127.\n\n## Changes\n\n**Request 1: the transactional Doublets row at 10M**\n\n- `Doublets_United_NonVolatile_Transactional` (Rust, opt-in `links` variant) puts the united file-mapped store behind doublets' `TransactionsDecorator`, with the shipped `FileTransitionLog`, which calls `sync_all` after every record.\n- The journal policy is left exactly as shipped. Each lifecycle phase that writes is one transaction: it begins at the phase's first write and commits at the phase's end, so the read phases begin none.\n- It is published next to `SQLite File` (stock defaults, `synchronous=FULL`) in a new \"Durable file storage\" section at 10,000,000 links, 32 and 64 bit, with `--repetitions 1`.\n- The plain `NonVolatile` rows are now described as \"file-backed without durability guarantees\" in both READMEs.\n\n**Request 2: SQLite's configuration**\n\n- A new `SQLite File Tuned` row runs `PRAGMA cache_size = -1048576; PRAGMA mmap_size = 1073741824;` before the schema is created.\n- It exists in Rust (`SQLite_File_Tuned`) and in both C# providers (`SQLite_File_Tuned` on Microsoft.Data.Sqlite, `SystemDataSQLite_File_Tuned` on System.Data.SQLite).\n- The file-backed Doublets rows are compared with it wherever it was measured.\n\n**Request 3: memory pressure**\n\n- `SQLite_File`, `Doublets_United_NonVolatile` and `Doublets_Split_NonVolatile` (32 bit) run inside a `systemd-run --scope` with `MemoryMax`, `MemorySwapMax=0` and `--repetitions 1`:\n  - 24 MiB at 1,000,000 links;\n  - 240 MiB at 10,000,000 links.\n- Under pressure a store can take hours, so each storage runs in its own job of one run. The report merges the jobs' reports into one table per limit, labelled with the limit, after checking that they share the run, the commit, the software and the configuration.\n- A second table under each one shows every job's runner, disk latencies, cgroup `memory.peak` and major page faults. The provenance line shows `memory.high` and the dirty page thresholds.\n- Both configured kinds record the disk the stores use: the median `O_DIRECT` random 4 KiB read latency and the `fsync` latency.\n- The READMEs state that the transactional store cannot take part, because its decorator keeps every transition and a full snapshot of the links in memory. The report validation rejects a memory-limit report that contains it.\n\n**Pipeline**\n\n- `.github/workflows/configurations.yml` plans and runs the configured jobs.\n- `scripts/benchmark_configuration.py` provides `plan`, `probe`, `record` and `report`. The configured reports are kept in `docs/benchmarks/configurations` and validated separately from the default reports, and the README sections are generated from them.\n- Pull requests run a small smoke plan. The published tables come from runs on this branch (see Validation).\n- A memory-limited job gives its storage `minutes` (a dispatch input, at most and by default 340), then stops it with `timeout`. The benchmark's `--phases` log keeps the phases it finished, and `benchmark_configuration.py unfinished` turns that log into the store's report.\n- `scripts/memory_limit_run.sh` samples the scope after a minute and then every 15 minutes: the benchmark's state and wait channel, its file, dirty and writeback pages, major faults, and memory and I/O pressure. At the end it writes `memory.peak`, `memory.stat` and `memory.events`, which outlive an OOM kill.\n\n**Latest dependencies**\n\n| Dependency | Version |\n| --- | --- |\n| doublets (Rust) | 0.21.0 |\n| platform-mem | 0.4.0 |\n| rusqlite | 0.43.0, bundling SQLite 3.54.1 |\n| Platform.Data.Doublets | 1.0.0 |\n| Platform.Data.Doublets.Sequences | 0.6.5 |\n| Microsoft.Data.Sqlite | 11.0.0, bundling SQLite 3.53.4 |\n| System.Data.SQLite | 2.0.4 |\n\n- doublets 0.21.0 fixes the 0.5.0 growth and split self-reference bugs, so those workarounds are removed. `experiments/unit_store_growth` and `experiments/split_store_delete` pass on it.\n- `Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL` 11.0.0 targets only `net11.0`, according to its NuGet catalog entry, so it stays at 10.0.3 on `net10.0`.\n- `link-cli` and `links-notation` are not used by this repository, so there is nothing to bump.\n- The Rust and C# tables use different SQLite engine versions (3.54.1 and 3.53.4), as bundled by their providers. The provenance lines record both.\n\n## Upstream bugs reported, with the workarounds kept here\n\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/issues/95: file-backed stores write zeros over every reservation, because `grow_filled` runs over a `set_len` extension. That is 32 MiB of dirty pages per growth of a 32-bit united store, so the 24 MiB run was OOM-killed before its first measured link.\n  - Workaround: `rust/src/memory.rs` `ZeroExtended` reports the extension as initialized, so the reservation stays a hole.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/issues/94: the split store's linked list of internal sources (`USE_LIST`) is unimplemented (`todo!()`). The Rust split store uses trees, unlike the C# default, and the READMEs say so.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets/issues/576: C# `Delete(id)` without a reset leaves stale index entries.\n  - Workaround: the harness still calls `Delete(id, handler: null)`. `experiments/csharp_delete_minimal` and `experiments/csharp_tree_delete` reproduce the bug on 1.0.0.\n- https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets/issues/577: the united store's size-balanced trees degenerate when many links share a source. It is documented, and the C# united store uses the AVL trees.\n\n## Memory-limit OOM root causes\n\nThe 24 MiB job was killed twice, for two different reasons. The kernel stats are in the job logs.\n\n1. **Zero-filled reservation** (doublets-rs#95 above): the reservation was written over with zeros. Fixed by `ZeroExtended`.\n   - `mapped_stores_do_not_write_their_reservation_and_reopen_with_their_links` checks on Linux that the reservation stays unallocated and that the store reopens with its links.\n   - On APFS the extension is allocated anyway (macOS 15, run 45603348935), so the check runs on Linux only, where the memory-limit runs happen.\n2. **Dirty and writeback pages that reclaim cannot free.** Each setting below was tried in a dispatch of the 24 MiB, 1M-link table. The job logs have the scope samples and the final `memory.stat` and `memory.events`.\n\n   | Setting | Run | Outcome |\n   | --- | --- | --- |\n   | Kernel defaults, `vm.dirty_ratio` 20%, `vm.dirty_background_ratio` 10% | [45604850024](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45604850024) | United store killed (`oom_kill 1`): 21.6 MiB of file pages, all dirty, 15.7 MiB under writeback. |\n   | `vm.dirty_bytes` and `vm.dirty_background_bytes` at 20% and 10% of the limit | [45681559798](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45681559798) | Every store, SQLite too, waited in `balance_dirty_pages` with I/O pressure and no memory pressure. |\n   | `vm.dirty_ratio` 5%, `vm.dirty_background_ratio` 2% | [45683252380](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45683252380) | SQLite and the split store run under real memory pressure (read waits, major faults). The united store was killed 4 s into `create`: 23.3 MiB of file pages, all under writeback. |\n   | The same, plus `strict_limit` on the storage disk's bdi | [45685437372](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45685437372) | No kill, but the mapped stores were throttled in `balance_dirty_pages` to about 3 MiB of file pages in 6 minutes, with no memory pressure. |\n   | The same ratios, plus `memory.high` at 7/8 of the limit (kept) | [45687063141](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45687063141) | No kill (`max 0`, `oom_kill 0`), peak at most 21.8 MiB. All three stores run under memory pressure: the united store had 448,638 major faults in 6 minutes. |\n\n   - Byte thresholds: for a cgroup, `domain_dirty_limits` in `mm/page-writeback.c` converts byte thresholds into a ratio of the runner's available memory, rounded up to 1/4096 (\"The byte settings can't be applied directly to memcg domains. Convert them to ratios by scaling against globally available memory.\"). It then applies that ratio to the memory the cgroup can use, so under 24 MiB the cgroup's thresholds came to a few pages. Earlier commits of this PR described the byte values as the cgroup's thresholds, which was wrong.\n   - Ratios alone: `balance_dirty_pages` compares the cgroup's dirty and writeback pages with its thresholds using `mem_cgroup_wb_stats`. That function reads the memcg counters after `mem_cgroup_flush_stats_ratelimited` (`mm/memcontrol.c`), and the counters are flushed every 2 s (`FLUSH_TIME`). In that window the united store, at about a microsecond per link, dirtied the whole limit. Reclaim cannot free pages under writeback, so the charge failed. This explanation comes from the kernel sources (v6.11) and the stats above. It was not confirmed with a kernel trace.\n   - `memory.high`: a task above it reclaims and sleeps on its way back to user space (`mem_cgroup_handle_over_high`), which gives the writeback time to finish before `memory.max`. The limit stays `memory.max`, and `memory.high` is recorded in the report and shown in the provenance line.\n\n## Reproduction and regression coverage\n\n- Rust (`rust/tests/storages.rs`):\n  - `every_optional_links_variant_passes_the_lifecycle` runs the tuned and transactional variants through the checked lifecycle.\n  - `transactional_store_commits_one_transaction_per_written_phase` and `transactional_store_journals_writes_outside_a_phase_one_by_one` read the journal entries.\n  - `mapped_stores_keep_their_links_when_their_memory_grows` and the reservation test above cover growth.\n- C# (`StoragesTests.cs`): `SQLiteVariantsAreRegistered` and `TunedSQLiteFilesApplyThePragmas` read the pragmas back from both providers.\n- Python (`scripts/test_benchmark_configuration.py`, `scripts/test_benchmark_report.py`) covers:\n  - plan validation, with one job per storage under a limit, the disk probe, cgroup stats parsing and recording, including the dirty thresholds, which are refused for a durable report;\n  - merging the per-storage reports of one table in the configured order, and refusing reports from different runs, duplicated storages, a table without `SQLite File` and duplicated durable reports;\n  - rejection of invalid configured reports (the transactional store under a limit, a missing limit or latency, invalid thresholds);\n  - the rendered sections in both languages;\n  - an exact match between the committed READMEs and the generator.\n\nRun the configured benchmarks locally as described in README \"Configured benchmarks\". Regenerate the READMEs with:\n\n```sh\npython scripts/benchmark_report.py docs/benchmarks/results \\\n  --configurations docs/benchmarks/configurations \\\n  --readme README.md --readme README.ru.md --charts docs/benchmarks\n```\n\n## Validation\n\n**Durable tables** ([run 45604850024](https://github.com/linksplatform/Comparisons.SQLiteVSDoublets/actions/runs/45604850024)):\n\n- Measured on PR head 4caf6c2, merged with `main` 870ddc7, on an Intel Xeon 6975P-C runner, 32 and 64 bit.\n- Since that run, the only Rust changes are in `rust/src/harness.rs` and `rust/src/main.rs`.
